sens: descendants de Jakin, fils de Siméon
H3200.detail: 1. The Jakinites are the members of the family clan descended from Jakin, son of Simeon. This clan is counted among the families of the sons of Simeon during the census of the people of Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 26:12). Jakin himself is mentioned for the first time in Genesis 46:10, when Jacob and his family go down to Egypt.
H3200.origine: The word Jakinites derives from the proper name Jakin (יָכִין), which means "he will establish." This name belongs to the lineage of the twelve sons of Simeon. In Genesis 46:10, Jakin appears among the children of Simeon born in Canaan before the descent into Egypt, and in 1 Chronicles 4:24, he is also called Jarib.
H3200.emploi: The Jakinites are mentioned only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:12, during the second census of the Israelites in the wilderness, after the exodus from Egypt. At that time, Moses takes inventory of the families of each tribe, and the family of the Jakinites is listed among the four families descended from the sons of Simeon. This administrative record shows how the clans of Israel were organized and counted for the journey in the wilderness and the future distribution of the land.

sens: Woman from the royal family of Judah in the 8th century B.C.
Wife of King Amaziah
Mother of King Uzziah (Ozias)
H3203.detail:
1. Jecolia is a woman mentioned twice in the Bible, always in connection with the kings of Judah. Her name appears during the accession to the throne of her son Uzziah, as reported in 2 Kings 15:2 and 2 Chronicles 26:3, which specify that she was from Jerusalem.

2. She is the wife of King Amaziah of Judah, who reigned before her son Uzziah. Therefore, she belongs to the royal lineage of the Southern Kingdom.

3. Her main role in the biblical narrative is to be the mother of King Uzziah, who reigned for fifty-two years in Jerusalem — one of the most significant kings of Judah before the exile. The two passages that mention her emphasize this royal motherhood.
H3203.origine: The name Jecolia means "God is able" or "God can." It is formed from the divine name Jehovah and a Hebrew verb expressing ability or strength. This name reflects the faith of the royal parents who expected their child to accomplish great things — which the history of her son Uzziah confirmed.
H3203.emploi: Jecolia appears only twice in the Bible, always in the same formula presenting the genealogy of the kings of Judah. She is named during the account of the beginning of her son Uzziah's reign in 2 Kings 15:2 and in 2 Chronicles 26:3. These two passages use the same terms, highlighting the importance of preserving the memory of the king's mother in the royal succession. She is identified as being from Jerusalem.
H3203.portee: The mere fact that Jecolia is named among the genealogies of the kings illustrates the importance of women in the continuity of the royal lineage and the people of God. Although few details are given about her, her mention honors the role of mothers in the history of salvation and reminds us that God uses entire families to accomplish His plan.

sens: King of Judah, son of Jehoiakim
Young king deported to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar
H3204.detail: Jeconiah is the name of a king of Judah, son of King Jehoiakim. He reigned for only three months and ten days before being captured and deported to Babylon (Jeremiah 24:1 mentions his deportation along with that of the leaders and craftsmen of Judah). Nebuchadnezzar imprisoned him in Babylon for thirty-six years, until the death of the Babylonian king; he was then released and lived the rest of his life in exile (1 Chronicles 3:16-17 places him in the royal lineage of Judah, and Esther 2:6 situates him among the great captives of war).
H3204.origine: The name means "The Lord will establish" in Hebrew. Jeconiah is also called Jehoiachin ("The Lord establishes"), and in the book of Jeremiah, he is referred to by the nickname Coniah (a shortened form). This king bears these name variants because his life was marked by the expectation of divine restoration, even after the humiliation of captivity.
H3204.emploi: Jeconiah appears seven times in the Bible, primarily in the historical and prophetic books of the turn of the 6th century B.C. The passages in 1 Chronicles place him in the royal genealogy of Judah and note that Assir and Shealtiel are his sons (1 Chronicles 3:17). The book of Esther (2:6) mentions him as one of the great ones taken captive. Jeremiah speaks of him several times: during his actual deportation (24:1), during the events of the captivity (27:20 and 28:4), showing that this captive king remains a central figure in the prophecies of restoration. Jeremiah 28:4 contains a promise that the Lord will bring him back from Babylon.
H3204.portee: Jeconiah embodies the fall and humiliation of the kingdom of Judah: from a legitimate king to a prisoner in exile. However, his survival and partial release symbolize the hope that God does not permanently reject His people, even in judgment. Through his descendants (notably Shealtiel), he figures in the genealogical line that leads to Jesus Christ according to Matthew 1:11, showing that even exile and political failure cannot annul God's promises for restoration and redemption.

sens: To give birth, to bring forth a child
To procreate, to conceive and give life
To beget, to be the origin of something or someone
To be born, to come into the world
To produce with effort or difficulty, as in childbirth
H3205.detail:
1. To give birth, to bring forth: this is the physical act of birth. The woman "gives birth" to the child she carries (Genesis 3:16: "you will give birth in pain"). This is the most concrete image of the word.
2. To procreate, to conceive: this means to beget a child, to create it through marital relations. Sarah "will give birth" to Isaac from God (Genesis 17:21), and Joseph saw his grandchildren "born" on his knees (Genesis 50:23).
3. To beget in a genealogy: this means to produce a descendant. In Hebrew, it is said that a father "begets" a son in the sense of the succession of generations (1 Chronicles 6:10: "Johanan begot Azariah").
4. To be born, to come into the world: the word also designates the action of the one who is born, not just that of the one who gives birth. A child "is born" of a father and a mother.
5. To produce with pain: the word can also express a painful or difficult production, as when it is said that someone "gives birth" to evil or iniquity (the image is that of childbirth in suffering).
H3205.origine: The word comes from an ancient Hebrew root that expresses the idea of giving birth. The root is related to the child ("yeled" in Hebrew) and the concept of generation. The word is used in all senses: to carry a child, to bring it into the world, and also to beget in a broad sense (to have descendants). The family of this word goes back to the very origins of the Semitic language.
H3205.emploi: This verb is very frequent in the Bible (403 occurrences), especially in Genesis where it structures the genealogies of the patriarchs (Genesis 5 and 10-11 repeat it incessantly). It primarily denotes the act of giving birth in the physical sense (Genesis 3:16, 4:1-2), then becomes a common genealogical verb to enumerate descendants ("A begot B"). It is also found in laments or poetic images: someone can "give birth" to suffering or sin in a figurative sense. Translations vary according to the context: "to give birth" or "to beget" for the biological act, "to be born" when it is about the subject who is born, "birth" when the meaning is nominal.
H3205.portee: This word reminds us that life comes from God and is transmitted. It celebrates childbirth as a blessed reality (Genesis 1:28), but also as a reality marked by pain since sin (Genesis 3:16). For the believer, "to give birth" evokes the transmission of spiritual life as well: Christ "gives birth" to His people, the Church brings Him forth. It is a word that honors motherhood and fatherhood as divine gifts.

sens: Little boy or small child, boy or girl at a young age
Son or daughter, descendant
Young man or boy in adolescence or early adulthood
Young people in the sense of courtiers or warriors in the service of a king
Descendants, posterity of a person
Figurative image: the people of Israel as children of God
H3206.detail:
1. The small child: the word primarily refers to the small child or infant, as in Moses saved from the waters (Exodus 2:6) or the child whom Elisha resurrects by covering him with his body to restore warmth and life (1 Kings 17:21-23).
2. The son or daughter in the family: this is a child or descendant in a broad sense, such as the children of Abraham or those that Hagar is to bear for Jacob (Genesis 30:26; Genesis 33:5, where Jacob calls his children "those that God has given me").
3. The young man or boy: the word applies to one who has grown but has not yet reached full adulthood, like Lamech who kills a young man (Genesis 4:23), or David in his youth.
4. Young people in the service of the king: Rehoboam "consulted the young men who had grown up with him and who surrounded him" (1 Kings 12:8), advisors in the sense of courtiers or young warriors.
5. The descendants or posterity of a person, their children and their children's children: when speaking of the children of a nation or lineage.
6. Israel as a child of God in prophetic language (Isaiah 8:18: "Here I am, I and the children God has given me"), or the youth of Israel as the people to be educated.
H3206.origine: The Hebrew word יֶלֶד comes from a root that denotes the idea of being born and growing, hence the primary image of one who comes out of the womb and grows. The family of the word includes terms for giving birth, begetting, and the notion of growth and youth. In Greek, this word is often translated as τέκνον (tekhnon, "child, son") or παῖς (pais, "child, boy, servant"), depending on the context and the age in question.
H3206.emploi: The word אֶלֶד appears 76 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives and the prophets, with a high frequency in Genesis. It is first used to designate children in the strict sense, from newborns to adolescents: Moses as a child saved from the waters, the child that Elisha resurrects, the children of Jacob. It extends to mean "young man" or "young people" for adolescents and young adults, particularly advisors or warriors in the service of a king (Rehoboam consults the young men, 1 Kings 12:8). In Isaiah 9:5, "a child is born to us, a son is given to us" announces the one who will bear the weight of government. The context of Jesus' birth is significant: this verse speaks first of a child who grows and takes power. The meaning can also be figurative to designate descendants or the people of Israel as children of God.
H3206.portee: This word reminds us that a child is a gift from God and a sign of blessing in the Bible (Genesis 33:5: "the children that God has given me"). It also evokes weakness and fragility (Genesis 33:13: "you know that the children are delicate"), which invites compassion and tenderness. Finally, when the Bible calls Israel or the faithful "child of God," it expresses the idea of filiation, a trusting dependence on the Heavenly Father, and divine education.

sens: Girl or adolescent of marriageable age
Young woman with the energy and vitality of youth
Child or inhabitant of a place in a context of prosperity or restoration
H3207.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a young girl of marriageable age: a female child who has become nubile, to whom marriage can be proposed, as with Dinah in Genesis 34:4, when Shechem asks her father to give her to him as a wife.
2. It also evokes the young woman in her dignity and value: when Joel 3:3 reports that the enemy sold the young girl for wine, the text emphasizes the abomination of the crime — a precious human life reduced to nothing.
3. It can simply designate the young inhabitants of a prosperous place: in Zechariah 8:5, "the streets will be filled with young boys and young girls playing," the image paints a picture of peace, fertility, and joy restored after desolation.
H3207.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "child, boy": yeled. The form "yaldah" is its regular feminine. It is a simple and concrete word, without mystery: it names the young girl as she is seen, from puberty until marriage. No pejorative connotation; the word retains the tenderness of the word "child."
H3207.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to speak of a young girl in her corporeality and vulnerability. In Genesis 34:4, it designates Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, at the heart of a story of rape and shame. In Joel 3:3, in the midst of a lamentation over the ravages of war, it recalls the horror of the trafficking of human beings — young girls sold like cattle. In Zechariah 8:5, on the other hand, it paints a picture of messianic restoration: young girls play freely in the streets, a symbol of peace and new life. The word thus embodies several tones, from tragedy to hope.
H3207.portee: This word reminds the reader of the fragility and dignity of young girls, particularly in contexts of violence or social rupture. It also invites the believer to see in Zechariah's vision a promise of restoration: one day, the younger generations will be able to live in safety and joy. It is a call to defend the vulnerable and to hope for the peace of God's kingdom.

sens: The period of life when one is young, from early adolescence to adulthood
The time of physical strength and vigor
The moment of inexperience and carefreeness
The time when the heart is free and inclined to pleasures
H3208.detail:
1. Youth is primarily the age that follows childhood: it is the season of life when the body grows and strengthens. It appears in Psalm 110:3, where the youth of God comes to him "like dew," a poetic image of his freshness and constant renewal.
2. In a physical sense, it is the time when strength and ardor reign: Psalm 110:3 describes the people of God as "full of zeal," a youth vibrant with power for battle.
3. Youth is also the age of inexperience, where the heart still ignores the weight of consequences. Ecclesiastes 12:1 calls the young man to "rejoice" and to "walk according to the sight of his eyes," but immediately adds: "know that for all this God will bring you into judgment."
4. Finally, it is the dawn of life, the time of carefreeness and pleasures; but Ecclesiastes 12:2 reminds us soberly: "youth and the dawn are vanity," meaning they pass quickly and are not lasting.
H3208.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "yld" which means "to give birth" or "to be born." Youth is therefore literally the state of one who has just been born. This root also produces the word "yeled" (child). The term "yaldout" expresses less childhood itself than adolescence and youthful age, the stage that immediately follows.
H3208.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. It is concentrated in the wisdom writings (Ecclesiastes) and poetic psalms. In Ecclesiastes 12:1 and 12:2, it designates the time of youth to which the Ecclesiastes addresses, this time when carefreeness reigns but where God does not relax his judgment. In Psalm 110:3, it takes on a more positive and poetic hue, speaking of the youth of the people of God, an image of renewal and power. In all cases, youth is seen as a distinct and fleeting season of life.
H3208.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the gift and responsibility of youth. It is not a period without consequences: even in joy and carefreeness, God calls us to account. But it is also the time when life is full of strength and potential; recognizing its relative vanity does not diminish the necessity of using it wisely and in the fear of God.

sens: To come into existence by birth
To be born, to have come into the world at a specific time or place
H3209.detail:
1. The word describes the act by which a child comes into the world. It is the birth itself, the moment when someone begins to live. Pharaoh orders the killing of every boy who is born (Exodus 1:22), that is, who comes into the world.
2. The word can also refer to the state or fact of being born, particularly at a specific time, in a specific place, or under specific circumstances. The children born in the desert during the Exodus had not been circumcised (Joshua 5:5), and the son born to David and Bathsheba would die (2 Samuel 12:14).
H3209.origine: The Hebrew word יִלּוֹד comes from a root that evokes the action of giving birth and bringing forth. It is related to the verb "to bear" and is part of the family of Hebrew words that speak of generation and lineage. The meaning is concrete and direct: it simply denotes the biological event of birth.
H3209.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Old Testament, particularly in historical and prophetic accounts. It is used to describe the coming into the world of ordinary children (the son of David, Exodus 1:22) as well as entire communities (the children born during the Exodus, Joshua 5:5). The context is often dramatic or significant: the birth of a royal heir (2 Samuel 5:14), the foretold birth of children promised in famine (Jeremiah 16:3). The word remains simple and factual, without moral connotation; it merely states the biological fact.
H3209.portee: This verb reminds us that every life, every birth is an event that God sees and that fits into His plan. It also emphasizes how precious life is from its very beginning: Pharaoh seeks to destroy the newborns, which shows the value that God places on each existence. For the reader, it is an invitation to recognize in every child a being that God brings into existence.

sens: A character from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible
H3210.detail: Jalon is a man from the tribe of Judah, living during the time of the divided monarchy (after the split of the kingdom of Israel). He is mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 4:17, where he appears in a genealogy as one of the sons of Ezra, brother of Jether, Mered, and Epher. His name literally means "God lodges" or "God establishes His dwelling," evoking the divine presence that remains. Although it is a simple genealogical name, it bears witness to a family of the people of Judah and its place in the history of the chosen people.
H3210.origine: The name Jalon comes from Hebrew and means "God (Yah) establishes His dwelling" or "God lodges" (from roots suggesting the idea of dwelling or settling). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God within it, like many Hebrew names. These names reflect the faith of the parents and their prayers for their children.
H3210.emploi: Jalon appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:17. He is listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, enumerated among the descendants of Caleb through his younger branch. This unique mention in the genealogical records of Chronicles shows that, although forgotten by the general history of Israel, each descendant of Judah had his place recorded in the memory of God's people.

sens: A person born of parents, resulting from a birth
A son or descendant of a person or family
A slave or servant born in the house of a master
A member of a race or warrior lineage
H3211.detail:
1. The word primarily designates one who has come into the world, resulting from a natural birth. In Genesis 17:12-13, the Law commands the circumcision of "the one born in your house": this is the child of the master, born of his parents or his servants, as opposed to one bought from outside.
2. It extends to any descendant of a person, especially when one wants to emphasize direct lineage. Thus, the three "children of Anak" (Numbers 13:22) are the sons of the giant Anak: the word indicates that they inherit his strength and monstrous nature.
3. In ancient households, a slave or servant born to the master, and who was part of the household from birth. Abram had "three hundred eighteen servants born in his house" (Genesis 14:14): these are his generational slaves, who belonged to him by right.
4. The word can designate a member of a race or a warrior clan transmitted by birth. The "children of Rapha" (2 Samuel 21:18) are the descendants of an ancient race of giants, identified by their origin.
H3211.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root יָלַד (yalad), which means "to bear, to give birth." It is a key word for speaking of generation and lineage: it is found in "יֶלֶד" (yeled) (child), "יָלְדָה" (yaldah) (daughter), and of course in compound names like "Ben..." (son of). The Hebrew word expresses a bodily and genealogical reality: one who is born shares the blood and heritage of those who have begotten him.
H3211.emploi: The word appears 13 times in biblical Hebrew, mainly in the Pentateuch and historical books. It first appears in the context of the Law (Genesis 17, Leviticus 22), to distinguish the children born in the house from those who came from outside. Then in the accounts of conquest (Numbers 13, Joshua 15), it names the giants or their races: the children of Anak are formidable adversaries. It is also found for soldiers or household servants (Genesis 14:14, 2 Samuel 21). Finally, in Jeremiah 2:14, the word takes on a metaphorical hue, applied to Israel itself to emphasize its birthright connection with God. The meaning varies little: it always refers to markers of generation, lineage, or belonging to a household.
H3211.portee: This word reminds the believer of the importance of origin and birth in biblical thought. For Israel, being born of Abraham means inheriting the promise. It also invites reflection on what it means to be "born" a child of God: not by accident, but by the intention of the Father who has chosen and begotten us. It is a word of lineage, legitimacy, and recognized place in a household and a covenant.

sens: To utter plaintive cries, prolonged and painful sounds expressing suffering
To express distress or sorrow through lamentations
To lament collectively in the face of misfortune or disaster
To express the mourning or affliction of a nation or community
H3213.detail:
1. The verb primarily describes the physical act of producing cries or prolonged groans: it is a sound of suffering that comes from the heart of the body. In Isaiah 13:6, the prophet calls to groan in the face of the day of the Lord's judgment.
2. These cries express an inner state of distress or sorrow. In Jeremiah 25:34, the shepherds are invited to groan because they will be slaughtered: their groaning is a sign of their anguish and loss.
3. The word is often used to describe the collective laments of a city or nation in the face of disaster. In Amos 8:3, the joyful songs of the palace become groans when judgment arrives, expressing the public sorrow of a defeated people.
4. By extension, to groan can mean to express mourning, national affliction, or moral prostration in the face of catastrophe: it is the voice of a community mourning its destruction or shame.
H3213.origine: The Hebrew verb יָלַל (yalal) expresses the idea of emitting a cry or noise. Its root evokes a sharp and repeated sound, similar to the cries made by distressed animals or humans in extreme suffering. The word belongs to the family of vocal expression and lamentation verbs in Hebrew. In Greek of the Septuagint, it is often translated as ὀλολύζω (ololuzo), which captures the idea of a piercing and prolonged cry well.
H3213.emploi: This verb appears 28 times in the Old Testament, primarily among the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Hosea, Joel) and always in the context of catastrophe, judgment, or mourning. It describes the reaction of peoples, cities, or communities in the face of invasion, destruction, loss, or divine judgment. In Isaiah 16:7, Moab groans for itself because of its ruin. In Jeremiah 48:39, the phrase "Let them groan" accompanies the collapse of a nation. The word always expresses deep and collective pain, never individual or light. It is a call to lamentation or a description of the affliction that accompanies the prophesied judgments.
H3213.portee: This word reminds the reader that suffering will find a voice, and that sin has visible and audible consequences: laments are the sound of judgment. For the believer, it invites recognition of the seriousness of sin and to take prophetic warnings seriously. Groaning is not a weakness, but the honest expression of loss and mourning in the face of what is broken.

sens: The piercing and frightening cry of wild beasts
The wild noise of a deserted and hostile place
H3214.detail:
1. The howl is the cry of wild animals — that of the wolf, the lion, or other beasts that terrify. It is a piercing, prolonged sound that resonates in the night and chills the blood. In Deuteronomy 32:10, God finds Israel in the midst of a solitude "with dreadful howls," where dangerous creatures reign.
2. By extension, the word designates the hostile and threatening atmosphere of a wild region where man cannot survive alone. The howls evoke total isolation, the absence of protection, the visceral fear produced by a desert populated by predators. It is the very noise of danger that surrounds it.
H3214.origine: The Hebrew word yélel comes from a root that imitates the cry itself: the sounds "yl" reproduce the high-pitched and whining tone of the animal howl. It is an onomatopoeic word, like many in ancient languages. The context of Deuteronomy suggests that this howl belongs to the wild and untamed life.
H3214.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 32:10. It is found in the song of Moses, where the poet paints the picture of the hostile desert in which God discovered Israel, nomadic and helpless. Israel was alone in a barren land, surrounded by dreadful howls of beasts, when God came to care for him tenderly. The word underscores the contrast between extreme danger and divine protection.
H3214.portee: This verse teaches that God fears nothing that frightens man: neither the desert, nor wild beasts, nor total isolation. He finds Israel precisely where everything seems hostile and comes to surround him with maternal care. For the believer, this text reminds us that God finds and protects us even when we are vulnerable and afraid, in a world that terrifies us.

sens: A cry of pain, a prolonged and loud complaint
The sound of a voice that groans, that howls under the effect of suffering
The collective expression of mourning and distress in a community
H3215.detail:
1. A lamentation is first and foremost a cry — but not just any cry: it is a sound of suffering, a groan or a howl that expresses intense pain. In Isaiah 15:8, the "lamentations" of Moab resonate across the borders, as if the earth itself were crying under the weight of misfortune.
2. The word also designates the noise made by voices that weep, groan, or cry out in despair. In Jeremiah 25:36, the shepherds let out "groans" because the Lord ravages their pastures: these are the complaints of those who see their lives collapsing.
3. In a communal sense, lamentation becomes the expression of collective mourning: it rises from the people in the face of disaster. Zephaniah 1:10 speaks of "lamentations" that resonate in the city on the day of judgment, as if the pain were shared by all.
H3215.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that suggests the cry, the sound of complaint. It belongs to the family of words of distress and calls for help. In Hebrew, the different forms of this root all express intense vocalization, whether it be a howl, a groan, or a cry of alarm. It is a vivid, concrete word that paints the scene rather than describing it abstractly.
H3215.emploi: The word appears four times in the Bible: in Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zephaniah, and Zechariah, all prophets. It always designates the sound of suffering in the face of misfortune: destruction of Moab, ravaging of flocks, day of judgment, ruin of magnificence. Sometimes it is the cry of the shepherds, sometimes that of an entire city, sometimes that of the earth itself. The image is always one of pain that cannot be silenced, that must be expressed through noise and howling.
H3215.portee: For the Christian reader, lamentation reminds us that suffering has a voice and deserves to be heard. It also shows that sin and judgment produce visible, audible, collective consequences. The Bible does not hide pain; it affirms it, describes it with its cries. This invites the believer not to stifle their own pain, but to bring it before God — as the Psalms teach.

sens: To say something without thinking, without weighing one's words
To make a decision or promise on a whim, without seriousness
To swallow one's words, or to let slip an impulsive word
H3216.detail:
1. The word describes the action of speaking in a hurried and thoughtless manner, as if the words escape uncontrollably. It is a word that has not been matured or weighed before being spoken. In Proverbs 20:25, the wise man warns that it is a trap to take a sacred commitment lightly, that is, to make a vow without truly reflecting on it.
2. By extension, the term refers to the act of committing or promising without seriousness, on the fly. The danger lurks for one who shouts "yes" or "I swear" without first contemplating what it costs. This contrasts with the proverb: the lightness of the moment clashes with the gravity of a promise made to God.
3. The underlying image is that of words flowing, that "flow" out of the mouth without a filter — hence the connection with the idea of swallowing or letting something slide without restraint.
H3216.origine: The Hebrew verb yaʿal carries the image of a word or action that escapes, flowing without being restrained. The root evokes the idea of something passing quickly, without reflection or control. The word stands in opposition to biblical wisdom, which values deliberation and caution before speaking or committing.
H3216.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 20:25. It is used there to describe the lightness with which one can treat a vow or promise made to God. The wisdom context of the Proverb emphasizes that this lightness is not trivial: it constitutes a trap. The wise man warns that taking a sacred commitment lightly places one in spiritual danger, for God takes seriously the promises made to Him.
H3216.portee: This word invites the believer to take seriously their commitments to God and to others. It teaches us that words have weight, and that we must think before swearing or promising. By showing us the trap of lightness, Wisdom calls us to caution and integrity: to say what we mean, and especially not to swear without counting the cost.

sens: Skin condition characterized by scaly patches or crusts
Skin disease considered a ritual impurity disqualifying the afflicted person
H3217.detail:
1. Scab is a skin disease that manifests as scaly patches, crusts, or flakes. It is a visible and recognizable condition, as seen in Leviticus 21:20 where it is listed among the physical defects enumerated.
2. In Israelite law, scab renders a person ritually impure and excludes them from worship: a priest afflicted with scab cannot approach the altar (Leviticus 21:20), and an animal offered as a sacrifice must not bear it (Leviticus 22:22). It is treated as a disqualifying impurity, on par with blindness or infirmities.
H3217.origine: The Hebrew word יַלֶּפֶת comes from a root meaning to flay or peel: it literally evokes a detached, scaly, or peeled skin. Scab is thus a disease where the skin loses its integrity and partially disintegrates, making it an image of degeneration.
H3217.emploi: The word appears twice in the Torah, in the two passages that outline the rules of Levitical purity. In Leviticus 21:20, it disqualifies a priest from divine service. In Leviticus 22:22, it invalidates an animal victim for sacrifice. Scab is thus systematically associated with ritual impurity and rejection; it is always a condition that excludes. It reflects the biblical conception that worship requires physical integrity, and that anything fragmented, scaly, or defiled is inaccessible to the approach of God.
H3217.portee: The mention of scab among the defects that exclude from divine service or invalidate the sacrifice shows that the Bible does not separate physical appearance from spiritual dignity: it demands wholeness and integrity. For the Christian reader, this reminds us that the Gospel breaks with this logic of exclusion—Jesus heals lepers and the infirm—but also that divine holiness requires respect and reverence.

sens: young locust or locust at an early stage of development
creature that devours and ravages
innumerable multitude
plague sent by God
H3218.detail:
1. The jélek is a young locust, probably at the stage where it actively feeds before its final transformation. This term designates a destructive insect par excellence, capable of devouring crops in a short time (Joel 1:4: "What the locust has left, the jélek has devoured").
2. The jélek appears as a devastator that leaves nothing in its wake. Its action of eating and ravaging is so complete that it becomes the very image of total destruction and ruin.
3. Like other species of locusts, the jélek advances in such crowds that they cannot be counted (Psalms 105:34: "Locusts without number"). This extreme abundance makes the jélek a symbol of the innumerable multitude.
4. In the Bible, the jélek is most often a plague that God sends to chastise His people or strike their enemies. It is a divine weapon that fills the heart with dread (Joel 2:25: "My great army that I sent against you").
H3218.origine: The word jélek comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of "licking" or "devouring," referring to how this insect consumes plants. Other related terms in the Bible also designate types of locusts: the gazam, the hasil, and the ordinary locust, but each at a different stage or variety. The jélek fits into a series of words to describe the different stages of the life cycle of locusts, a reality well known to farmers of the ancient Near East.
H3218.emploi: The jélek appears seven times in the Bible, mostly in prophetic texts. In the book of Joel (1:4 and 2:25), it is listed among other species of locusts as an agent of destruction sent by the Lord. Psalm 105:34 mentions it as a plague without number sent against Egypt. Jeremiah 51:14 and 51:27 compare it to countless soldiers assailing an enemy. In Nahum 3:15, we see the jélek destroying by fire. The term remains consistent in all these passages: it is always a devastating insect, sent or used as an image of an irresistible destructive force.
H3218.portee: The jélek reminds the reader that sin has visible and destructive consequences, and that God has powerful means to chastise. But it also shows that God can restore what has been destroyed: Joel 2:25 promises renewal after the devastation. This word thus invites the believer to fear God's judgment, but also to hope for His forgiveness and restoration.

sens: Small bag or compartment attached to clothing, used to carry and keep personal items
Satchel or pouch used as luggage or work equipment
H3219.detail: 1. A pocket is a small sewn or attached receptacle on clothing, intended to store items that one wants to have at hand. It is a safe place to keep precious or necessary things for daily life. In the account of David facing the Philistine, the young shepherd places the five carefully chosen stones in his pocket — a gesture that is both practical and symbolic, as this simple equipment is part of his armament when he steps forward without armor against Goliath (1 Samuel 17:40). 2. More broadly, the word refers to any small portable bag or satchel, the equipment of one who travels, works, or needs to keep their belongings with them. It is a humble yet indispensable utensil for the warrior, shepherd, or traveler.
H3219.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to gather" or "to collect" — the basic idea is a receptacle that gathers and holds together. The pocket is therefore literally what gathers and keeps together the small items entrusted to it. It is a humble word from the everyday vocabulary of the ancient Near East.
H3219.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Samuel 17:40. The occurrence is at the crucial moment when David prepares to face Goliath: he chooses his simple shepherd's equipment — a staff, a sling, and the stones kept in his pocket. This context shows that the pocket was an integral part of the daily equipment of an ordinary shepherd or warrior. The unique usage emphasizes the austerity of David's means, contrasting with the impressive armor of the giant.
H3219.portee: This detail about the pocket reveals how David prepares for battle: not with sophisticated equipment, but with the simple resources of the shepherd he is. It is a discreet lesson on faith: God does not ask for prestigious armaments, but for availability and courage. David's pocket, filled with five smooth stones, represents trust in God more than human warrior power.

sens: expanse of salty water, ocean or large inland sea
mass of water in general, river or large watercourse
basin or reservoir of water
direction of the west, side of the sea
crowd or multitude that stirs like the waves
H3220G.detail:
1. The sea is the vast expanse of salty water: the Mediterranean, the Red Sea, the Dead Sea, or the Sea of Galilee. In Genesis 1:10, God calls the gathered waters he created "seas" and finds it good. It is the biblical image of what is vast, deep, and powerful.

2. The sea also refers to any large watercourse, particularly the Nile: in 1 Kings 4:29, Solomon's wisdom is compared to the sand by the sea, symbolizing the countless. The mighty river can be called sea because it covers and sweeps away like the waves.

3. In the temple, the "sea" was a large bronze basin intended for the priests' ablutions — a reservoir of water in a concrete sense.

4. The word also means the direction of the west, the side where the sea is located: in Deuteronomy 3:17, the borders extend "to the sea" in the sense of towards the west.

5. Isaiah 17:12 speaks of the peoples that roar "like the roaring of the sea": here the sea figures the agitated, noisy, and tumultuous crowd that thunders and advances irresistibly.
H3220G.origine: The Hebrew word yam comes from an ancient root common to Semitic languages. The primary image is that of movement, of bubbling — the sea that moves and lives. In the Hebrew Bible, the sea is often associated with primordial chaos before creation, but it also becomes an element of beauty and power in God's created order. The family of the word covers all meanings of living and moving water.
H3220G.emploi: The word sea appears 281 times in the Old Testament, primarily in historical accounts, geographical descriptions, and poetry. Its usage changes according to the context: it is first a concrete geographical reality (the Mediterranean bordering Canaan in Genesis 49:13), then an obstacle or a mirror of divine power (Exodus 14, the crossing of the Red Sea becomes the sign of salvation), and finally a poetic and prophetic image of the agitation of nations or of the incomprehensible immensity (Psalms 24:2, Isaiah 17:12). The word can also designate the boundaries of the promised land and, in descriptions of the temple, the immense ritual basin.
H3220G.portee: The sea in the Bible is never neutral: it is both the domain of God's creative power and, at times, the symbol of danger or chaos. When God masters the sea (Exodus 14), he manifests his authority over the world and his salvation towards his people. For the believer, the sea reminds that there are realities greater than oneself, which call for trust in the power and goodness of the Creator.

sens: expanse of salty water, large liquid mass
the Mediterranean or other named seas
direction: the west, in relation to the Mediterranean shore
western side of a building or region
H3220H.detail: 1. The word primarily designates an expanse of salty water, a true sea: the Mediterranean bordering the land of Israel, the Red Sea that the Israelites crossed during the Exodus, the Dead Sea, or the Sea of Galilee. It is also a large basin, like the bronze one in the temple described in 1 Kings 7:25. 2. The Bible uses the same word to refer to the course of the Nile, a mighty river, showing that "sea" can apply to very large watercourses (Isaiah 24:14 evokes this broad sense). 3. Because the Mediterranean is located to the west of Israel, the word "sea" comes to simply mean "the west" or "the western side": Genesis 12:8 says that Abraham camped "with Bethel to the west," using this same word to indicate a direction. 4. Numbers 3:23 describes the Gershonite camp "behind the tabernacle to the west": this is a position, not a presence of water. The word is thus used for the western side of a region, city, or religious building (Ezekiel 47:20 situates "the western side" to delineate the restored temple).
H3220H.origine: The Hebrew word yam comes from a very ancient root associated with flow, with the movement of water. In biblical and post-biblical Hebrew, it remains the common term for any large body of water. Its use for "west" is explained by geography: for an Israelite settled in the center of the land, the Mediterranean is to the west, so that the words "sea" and "west" become almost interchangeable. This dual meaning illustrates how geography shapes language: the landscape becomes a compass.
H3220H.emploi: The word appears 67 times in the Hebrew Bible. It primarily designates large bodies of water: the Mediterranean (Joshua 5:1), the Dead Sea (Ezekiel 47:20), the Sea of Galilee (Joshua 12:7). It also appears in descriptions of the temple and its sacred objects: the large bronze basin in 1 Kings 7:25 and 2 Chronicles 4:4, called "the Sea." But the most common usage in the Bible remains the direction: dozens of verses use it to mean "the west" or "western," especially in passages delineating lands (Joshua and Ezekiel) and describing the camp of Israel at the stages of the desert (Numbers 2:18, 3:23). A single passage can mix both meanings: the text of Ezekiel about the restored temple alternates between "the great sea" (the true Mediterranean) and "the western side" (the direction).
H3220H.portee: This word enriches faith by revealing how God uses creation — seas, boundaries, the entire geography — to structure his plan. The seas that border the promised land mark God's love for Israel; they are also limits that remind of divine sovereignty. Understanding that "sea" also means "west" shows how the physical reality of the world shapes human language: God speaks to a people rooted in a concrete territory.

sens: large expanse of salt water
body of water that surrounds land
source of strange and threatening creatures
symbol of chaos and agitation
H3221.detail:
1. The sea is a large expanse of salt water that surrounds inhabited lands. In Daniel 7:2, the prophet sees "the four winds of heaven stirring up the great sea," evoking this vast aquatic surface that the winds can agitate.
2. By extension, it refers to the body of water itself, a powerful and moving natural element. In Daniel 7:3, "four great beasts came up from the sea," showing that the sea is the medium from which monstrous and terrifying creatures emerge.
3. In these two verses from chapter 7 of Daniel, the sea becomes a symbol of chaos, trouble, and instability — a space from which the unexpected and fearsome arise, in line with the prophetic vision of a disordered world before the establishment of God's kingdom.
H3221.origine: The Aramaic word יַם (yam) is closely related to the Hebrew יָם (yam, H3220), also meaning "sea." This Semitic root designates salt water, the main element of habitable land. The word appears in Aramaic in the later passages of the Bible, notably in Daniel, when the text shifts from the Hebrew historical context to prophetic visions of universal scope. The sea, in this context, is not just a geographical reality: it carries a symbolic weight of instability and power.
H3221.emploi: The word יַם appears twice in the Aramaic Bible, only in chapter 7 of Daniel. In these two instances, it designates the source of the four prophetic beasts that arise in verses 2 and 3. The sea is not just a backdrop: it is the primordial chaos from which hostile political and religious powers against God emerge. This image of the sea as the matrix of chaos is rooted in the older biblical tradition, where water often represents what is turbulent and uncontrollable. In Daniel's vision, it embodies the turmoil of nations and the agitation of the unbelieving world.
H3221.portee: This vision of the sea as the source of chaos invites the Christian reader to recognize that the political and human powers opposing God emerge from a moral and spiritual instability. It also reminds believers, faced with the agitation of the world, to set their gaze on God and the stable establishment of His kingdom, not on the deceptive waves of earthly events. The sea of Daniel 7 already announces what Revelation will confirm: that God controls all powers, even the most terrifying.

sens: spring of hot water that gushes from the ground
discovery or resource found in the desert
H3222.detail: 1. A hot spring is an accumulation of boiling water that naturally emerges from the ground, fed by underground heat. The word here designates a remarkable geological phenomenon: Ana discovered hot springs in the arid desert (Genesis 36:24), a valuable find in a dry land where water is rare and precious. 2. By extension, the term can also refer to any valuable discovery or resource found in desert lands. This makes Ana's mention notable: in a pastoral context where wealth is counted in livestock, finding hot springs in the desert is a remarkable success, worthy of remembrance.
H3222.origine: The Hebrew word יֵמִם (yem) has an uncertain meaning; scholars hesitate between several interpretations, including "hot springs" or possibly mules or other animals. Its precise etymology remains obscure. The Segond 1910 chose to translate it as "springs" or "hot springs," which fits well in the context of the desert where Ana was pasturing the flocks. This uncertainty about the original word shows that the ancient text has kept a mystery about the exact nature of Ana's discovery.
H3222.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 36:24, at the heart of a genealogy of the descendants of Esau. Ana, son of Zibeon, is mentioned as the one who "found the hot springs in the desert." This unique mention marks an otherwise obscure character with an extraordinary detail: the discovery of a rare resource in an arid land. It distinguishes Ana within the family lineage and underscores the importance of this find for the clan.
H3222.portee: This mention of Ana's discovery reminds us that even in seemingly dry genealogical passages, the Bible honors those who discover and develop the riches of the created world. It is a subtle invitation to recognize God's providence: a hot spring in the desert is a concrete blessing, a sign of His care for those who seek and work.

sens: Eldest son of Simeon, one of the twelve sons of Jacob
H3223.detail: Jemuel is the eldest son of Simeon, himself one of the twelve sons of Jacob. He appears in the list of Simeon's children who go down to Egypt with Jacob and his family. He is a figure from the early days of the people of Israel, living during the time of slavery in Egypt and the Exodus. He is the founder of one of the families of the tribe of Simeon. Although he is not extensively narrated in the text, he embodies the generations that make up the chosen people at the time when God is about to liberate them. In Numbers 26:12, he is also referred to as Nemuel.
H3223.origine: His name literally means "day of God." He is a historical figure in the traditions of the people of Israel, attested in the genealogical lists of Jacob's children. The Bible mentions him as a link in the chain of the chosen people, a descendant of Jacob and patriarch of one of the families that make up Israel. Although the name is not widely used in later history, his existence marks the importance of the multiplication of the offspring promised to Jacob.
H3223.emploi: Jemuel is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both times in the same places: he appears in the list of Simeon's sons in Genesis 46:10, when Jacob goes down to Egypt with his entire family, and again in Exodus 6:15, where the sons of Simeon are listed again. In both contexts, he is consistently cited first among the sons of Simeon, confirming that he is the eldest. In Numbers 26:12, the same character is called Nemuel. These two names refer to the same person, likely a spelling variant of the same tradition. He is the brother of Jamin, Ohad, Jakin, Tzochar, and Saul, all sons of Simeon, one of whose wives was a Canaanite woman.

sens: Daughter of Job
One of the three daughters born to Job after his restoration
Name meaning 'day by day' or 'dove'
H3224.detail: 1. Jemima is one of the three daughters that Job had after the Lord restored his life and prosperity (Job 42:14). She is the first named among these three daughters, before Ketsia and Kéren-Happuc. 2. Her Hebrew name יְמִימָה (yemimah) means 'day by day' or evokes the idea of beauty and regularity, similar to a dove. It was a name of dignity and hope, reflecting renewal and blessing in Job's life. 3. Although mentioned only once in the Bible, Jemima symbolizes divine restoration and God's generosity toward those who endure suffering with faith: after losing everything, Job receives not only new material wealth but also a new family, including these three daughters with significant names.
H3224.origine: The name Jemima comes from the Hebrew יָמִים (yamim), which means 'days'. The feminine suffix -ah makes it a female name. The original image is that of the regular succession of days, symbolizing continuity, constancy, and daily beauty. Some biblical scholars also see a connection with Aramaic, where the name would evoke a dove, a bird of gentleness and purity in biblical symbolism.
H3224.emploi: Jemima is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Job 42:14. She appears in the account of Job's final restoration, after he endured terrible trials and pleaded his case before God. God restores to him everything he had lost — his possessions, his health, and his family. The enumeration of Job's three daughters, with their beautiful names, highlights the abundance and grace of this restoration. Unlike Job's ten sons (mentioned in Job 1:2), Scripture takes care to name his three daughters, which was rare in the biblical context and shows their particular value in the eyes of the author and God.
H3224.portee: The mention of Jemima and her sisters reminds the reader that God restores not only the material goods and health of those who suffer faithfully but also family and joy. The names given to these daughters — Jemima ('day by day'), Ketsia ('cinnamon'), Kéren-Happuc ('horn of kohl') — testify to the beauty regained. For the believer, it is a promise that suffering does not have the final word, and that God honors those who persevere in faith.

sens: The right hand, or the right side of the body
The direction of right, as opposed to left
The south, geographical orientation when facing east
The position of honor or power beside someone
The idea of justice, victory, or strength
The act of standing firm, staying true to one's path
H3225G.detail:
1. The right hand, or the right side of the body — This is the concrete and primary meaning: the limb or side opposite to the left. In Hebrew, it is even the word used as a measure for gestures and positions: when Jacob places his right hand on Ephraim and his left hand on Manasseh (Genesis 48:14), we know exactly what gesture he is making. The term also covers the parts of honor in sacrifice: the right thigh belongs to the priest (Leviticus 7:32).
2. The direction of right, as opposed to left — Abraham tells Lot: 'If you go left, I will go right' (Genesis 13:9), simply designating a direction. The word is used to trace a path, a choice of route: Deuteronomy 2:27 speaks of 'not turning aside to the right or to the left' from a main road.
3. The south, geographical orientation when facing east — This is a logical extension: if one turns to face the east (the rising sun), the right indicates the south. This directional nuance appears in texts that describe the geography of Israel.
4. The position of honor or power beside someone — When one stands at the right hand of a king or judge, it is a place of authority and trust. An accuser stands at the right hand of the wicked to accuse him (Psalms 109:6). God places His enemies as a footstool under His right hand (Psalms 110:1).
5. The idea of justice, victory, or strength — In the Psalms, the right hand of God is the one that saves, crushes the enemy, and acts with power: 'Your right hand, Lord, has been glorified' (Exodus 15:6). It is the arm that executes judgments and wonders.
6. The act of standing firm, staying true to one's path — Not turning aside 'to the right or to the left' (Deuteronomy 5:32) means walking straight, remaining faithful to the path laid out, not deviating from the order received.
H3225G.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of firmness or straightening. The right hand is the one of strength and control for most humans, which explains its association with power, authority, and protection. In geographical context, the south derives its name from the fact that, facing east (a major cardinal direction), the right always designates this direction. The notion of honor and power associated with the right is universal in ancient cultures.
H3225G.emploi: The word appears more than 100 times in the Bible, especially in Exodus, the Psalms, and the historical books. It first describes the body and gestures (the right hand of sacrifices, Jacob's blessings). Then it becomes directional (not turning aside to the right or left from the path commanded by God). Finally, it takes on a strong theological dimension in the Psalms, where the right hand of God symbolizes His power, victory, and support for the righteous. Psalms 16:8 and 110:1 are major examples: 'The Lord is at my right hand' expresses trust in divine protection, while 'Sit at my right hand' describes the exaltation of the Messiah. Isaiah 9:19 shows that the word can also simply designate a side, that which suffers injustice and famine.
H3225G.portee: For the Christian, the right is primarily the sign of God's support and protection: knowing that the Lord is at one's right hand (as expressed in Psalm 23) is a source of confidence in trial. It is also the image of Christ's exaltation: the Father has placed Him at His right hand, as a sign of victory and sharing in His reign. Finally, not turning aside 'to the right or to the left' speaks to each person's conscience: faithfulness requires walking straight, without deviating out of greed or fear.

sens: The right hand or the right side of the body
The direction to the right
The south (the direction of the right when facing east)
The position of strength or honor
Help or support
H3225H.detail:
1. The right hand or the right side of the body: this is the limb or part of the body located on the right side. In the temple, the lampstands were placed "five on the right and five on the left" (2 Chronicles 4:7), marking a balanced symmetry around the sanctuary.
2. The direction to the right: when describing the orientation of a place or a path, "right" indicates the direction of the right side. Aroër was camped "to the right of the city" (2 Samuel 24:5), meaning on the right flank of that city.
3. The south, because when facing east (as was done in Israel), the right hand points south. Hakila is described as being in the "south of the desert" (1 Samuel 23:19), that is, to the south.
4. The position of strength or honor: the right hand is stronger and more skillful than the left. Psalms 89:13 speaks of the "right hand" of the Lord as a symbol of His power.
5. Help or support: one who stands at the right of another supports and protects him, an image of divine assistance.
H3225H.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that fundamentally means "the hand that acts, that works." The right is traditionally the hand of action, strength, and effectiveness. Related words express the idea of turning or directing. Because the geography of Israel is often oriented towards the east, the right naturally became a term to designate the south. In New Testament Greek, this word is translated as "dexios," which carries the same meanings.
H3225H.emploi: The word appears about fifteen times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical accounts and descriptions of the temple. It first denotes the literal sense: the physical hand or side (2 Chronicles 3:17 for the temple columns, 1 Kings 7:49 for the lampstands). It also indicates the geographical direction, particularly the south (1 Samuel 23:19). By extension, in the Psalms, it takes on a symbolic value of power and protection (Psalms 89:13). In all contexts, the word retains its concrete spatial meaning: it always designates what is placed or oriented towards the right, without ambiguity.
H3225H.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader visualize biblical scenes and grasp the descriptions of the temple accurately. When the Bible speaks of the "right hand of God," it evokes divine power and the Lord's protection for His people. It is a practical word that anchors biblical promises in concrete and reassuring images.

sens: second son of Simeon, ancestor of a family of Israel
the right hand (meaning of the name)
H3226G.detail:
1. Jamin is the second son of Simeon (son of Jacob). He is mentioned in the genealogical lists of Exodus and Numbers as the founder of the family of the Jaminites, which formed one of the twelve tribes of Israel (Numbers 26:12). His name, which means "the right hand," was a beneficial name in Hebrew culture, as the right hand symbolizes strength and favor.
2. The meaning of the name "right hand" evokes blessing and power, a common image in the Old Testament to designate what is strong and precious.
H3226G.origine: The name Jamin comes from the Hebrew root meaning "right hand" (יָמִין). It is a theophoric name that expresses a blessing or a desirable quality. It also appears as "Jaminite" (יָֽמִינִי) to designate the descendants of this son of Simeon.
H3226G.emploi: Jamin is mentioned four times in the biblical genealogical lists: first in Genesis 46:10 during Jacob's descent into Egypt, then in Exodus 6:15 and Numbers 26:12 in the enumerations of the sons of Simeon. There is also a mention in 1 Chronicles 4:24. These references show that Jamin was a revered ancestor whose descendants formed an officially recognized family of Israel, the family of the Jaminites.

sens: Son of Ram, of the tribe of Judah
H3226H.detail: Jamin is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible. He is designated as one of the sons of Ram the Jerahmeelite, alongside his brothers Maats and Eker (1 Chronicles 2:27). His name literally means "right hand" in Hebrew, which may suggest a blessing or a mark of favor, although the biblical texts tell us little about his personal life or role.
H3226H.origine: The name Jamin comes from the Hebrew יָמִין (yamin), which means "right hand." In biblical culture, the right symbolizes strength, favor, and blessing. This name was borne by several individuals in Israel's history: notably by the second son of Simeon, founder of the clan of the Jaminites (see Genesis 46:10), as well as by this Jamin of Judah and a Levite who helped Ezra interpret the Law. It is a theophoric name that expresses trust in divine protection.
H3226H.emploi: Jamin appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 2:27, where he is cited among the descendants of Judah through the lineage of Ram the Jerahmeelite. He is simply a member of the Davidic genealogy, with no particular event associated with his name. This brief genealogical passage shows that the Bible faithfully records the names of many people whose lives left no other written trace, reminding us that God knows each by name.
H3226H.portee: This forgotten character from the biblical accounts teaches us a lesson in humility: even those whose names appear only once were part of God's people and divine plan. The Bible does not report the great actions of everyone, but it carefully records genealogies, reminding us that every human life has value in the eyes of the Lord, whether in light or in darkness.

sens: Levite who helped Ezra explain the Law to the people
H3226I.detail: Jamin is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when Ezra gathers the people to read and explain the Law of Moses. Jamin is part of the Levites tasked with assisting in this public interpretation (Nehemiah 8:7), a fundamental work in restoring the religious life of Israel after the Exile.
H3226I.origine: The name Jamin means "right hand" in Hebrew, thus evoking strength, authority, or favor. This name has been borne by other individuals in the Old Testament (notably a son of Simeon), but here it designates a Levite during the Restoration.
H3226I.emploi: Jamin appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 8:7. He is mentioned among a group of Levites who, at the moment when Ezra publicly reads the Law before all the people in Jerusalem, stand up to explain and make it understandable to everyone. This event marks a key moment in the religious and communal reorganization after the return from Exile. His role shows the importance of the Levites as mediators and teachers of God's Word.

sens: Person from the tribe of Benjamin
Inhabitant of the territory of Benjamin
Warrior or soldier from the tribe of Benjamin
H3227B.detail:
1. A Benjamite is a person from the tribe of Benjamin, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. Benjamin was the youngest son of Jacob (also called Israel) and Rachel. In 1 Samuel 9:1, Kish is described as "a man of Benjamin" — he is a Benjamite, a member of this tribal family.

2. The word also refers to the region or territory inhabited by this tribe. In 1 Samuel 9:4, the text states that they "traveled through the land of Benjamin" — this refers to the geographical area in southern Israel where the descendants of Benjamin lived.

3. In a military context, the Benjamites are the warriors and soldiers of this tribe. In 1 Chronicles 27:12, "Abiezer, of Anathoth, a Benjamite" is mentioned as commanding a division of twenty-four thousand men — these are the fighting troops of Benjamin.
H3227B.origine: The word comes from Benjamin, the name of Jacob and Rachel's youngest son. His name means "son of the right hand" or "son of the south" in Hebrew. The term "Benjamite" (יְמִינִי) is derived from this tribal name, which designates all the descendants of Benjamin and the region they occupied after the conquest of Canaan.
H3227B.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. In 1 Samuel 9:1, it describes Kish, the father of Saul, the first king of Israel — thus establishing that Saul came from the tribe of Benjamin. In 1 Samuel 9:4, it refers to the region itself. In 1 Chronicles 27:12, it names the soldiers of Benjamin who served in the army organized by David. Benjamite is therefore a term of genealogical and geographical identification, anchoring characters and troops in their tribal origin.
H3227B.portee: Benjamin holds a special place in the history of Israel: he is the youngest son of Jacob, favored by his father, and his tribe produced Saul, the first king, and later the kingdom of Judah after the division. Recognizing someone as a Benjamite places them within a genealogy and tribal responsibility. For the Christian, this reminds us that God guides history through concrete families and peoples, with their particular traditions and calls.

sens: Person belonging to the tribe of Benjamin
H3228G.detail: 1. A Benjamite is a member of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. Benjamin is the youngest son of Jacob and Rachel, born in Canaan (Genesis 35:18). His descendants form a distinct tribe with their own lands and identity. In 2 Samuel 20:1, Sheba, a Benjamite, revolts against King David by blowing the trumpet and calling the Israelites to detach themselves from the royal house.
H3228G.origine: The word comes from the name Benjamin (בִּנְיָמִין), which literally means "son of the right hand" (bin = son, yamin = right hand). This name reflects the special blessing that Jacob bestowed upon this youngest son. The adjective Benjamite simply designates one who descends from Benjamin and belongs to his tribe. The tribe of Benjamin became famous in the history of Israel, particularly as the seat of the southern kingdom (Judah) after the division of the kingdom.
H3228G.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in 2 Samuel 20:1, where it designates Sheba as a Benjamite participating in the revolt against David. This passage shows how tribal identity remained important during the time of the monarchy, even after the unification of the country under David. Sheba is presented as a man who exploits his tribal affiliation to rally his compatriots against the central authority.
H3228G.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, tribal identity was fundamental to the social, political, and religious life of Israel. Each tribe possessed its territorial heritage and role within the people of God. Understanding these tribal distinctions helps to grasp the tensions and loyalties that structured Israelite society and the stakes of the conflicts recounted in the Old Testament.

sens: Descendants of Jamin, son of Simeon
H3228H.detail: The Jaminites are the members of the family clan descended from Jamin, who was one of the sons of Simeon (himself a son of Jacob). Jamin lived during the time of Egypt and the desert, and his descendants formed one of the families of the tribe of Simeon. In the census of the Israelites in the desert, reported in Numbers 26:12, the Jaminites are listed among the families descended from the sons of Simeon, alongside the Nemuelites, the Jachinites, and other groups.
H3228H.origine: The name Jaminites comes from Jamin (in Hebrew Yamin), which literally means "the right hand" or "right." It is a symbolic name borne by one of the twelve sons of Simeon. The suffix -ites (in Hebrew -im) classically designates the descendants or members of a family, creating a gentilice or ethnic term: the Jaminites are thus "those who come from Jamin."
H3228H.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:12, during the second census of Israel in the desert, after the exodus from Egypt. In this administrative and genealogical context, Moses counts all the families of each tribe to prepare for the division of the promised land. The Jaminites are presented as a minor branch of the tribe of Simeon, alongside other eponymous families descended from Jamin's brothers.

sens: Father of the prophet Micah during the divided monarchy
H3229.detail: Jimla is a man living at the time of the division of the kingdom of Israel, known only as the father of the prophet Micah. He appears in the account where King Ahab of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah seek prophets to consult the Lord. King Ahab mentions Micah by saying: "It is Micah, son of Jimla" (1 Kings 22:8 and its parallel in 2 Chronicles 18:7). Although Jimla himself never appears or is named elsewhere in the Bible, he is identified by his paternity of the prophet who had the courage to speak against Ahab.
H3229.origine: The name Jimla (יִמְלָה in Hebrew) literally means "he whom God will fill" or "that God will fill," composed of the root מלא (male, "to fill") and the personal suffix. This name expresses a divine blessing, an expectation that God will accomplish His purpose in this character or his family.
H3229.emploi: Jimla appears only 4 times in the Bible, always associated with the prophet Micah. The two parallel accounts — 1 Kings 22:8-9 and 2 Chronicles 18:7-8 — both mention "Micah, son of Jimla" to clearly identify him. Ahab, the king of Israel, recognizes Jimla's existence only to designate his son, the prophet whose words of curse he fears. The context is that of a prophetic consultation before a battle, where the other prophets promise victory while Micah brings a contrary word.
H3229.portee: Jimla reminds us that the servants of God — and here Jimla's son, Micah — often come from families whose name itself carries a divine promise. The contrast between Ahab's reluctance to listen to a prophet whose father is named "he whom God will fill" and the truth that this prophet brings invites the reader to recognize that God accomplishes His purposes through those He chooses, regardless of the prejudices of kings.

sens: Man from the tribe of Simeon during the divided monarchy
H3230.detail: Jamlec is a chief of the tribe of Simeon, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:34, in the genealogy of the descendants of Simeon. His name means "He will reign" in Hebrew, expressing a confidence or divine promise. No other details are given about his life or role.
H3230.origine: The name Jamlec comes from Hebrew and is composed of two elements: "jam" (he) and "mlek" (to reign). It is a theophoric name, meaning it expresses a belief or expectation towards God: the father of this man gave this name in the hope or affirmation that his son would reign or that God would reign. This type of name was common in Israel to express the faith of parents.
H3230.emploi: Jamlec appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:34. He is listed in the genealogical record of the chiefs of the tribe of Simeon, alongside Meshobab and Josha. This enumeration shows the importance of this family in the history of the tribe. The text explicitly designates him as chief, suggesting a role of political or religious leadership among the Simeonites. Beyond this mention, nothing else is known about him.

sens: To head towards the right, the right side
To use the right hand, to be right-handed
To choose the right side (in the figurative sense of direction or choice)
H3231.detail:
1. To head towards the right, the right side: this literally means to turn or move to the right rather than to the left. Abram tells Lot: "if you go left, I will go right" (Genesis 13:9), clearly indicating that they will take opposite directions and separate.
2. To use the right hand, to be right-handed: this meaning describes the action of using one's right hand to fight or work. The Benjamite archers could throw stones "with the right hand and the left hand" (1 Chronicles 12:2), demonstrating great skill.
3. To choose or turn towards the right side (figuratively): the word also expresses the idea of choosing or favoring a direction. The king commands the sword: "Turn to the right! […] Turn to the left!" (Ezekiel 21:21), indicating destructive power in all directions.
H3231.origine: The verb comes from the root יָמִין (yamin), which means "right" or "right hand" in Hebrew. The right side was historically associated with strength, honor, and blessing in Israelite culture: this is why it becomes a term of direction and orientation. The root is very ancient and appears in several Semitic languages with the same fundamental meaning.
H3231.emploi: This verb appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first used in the literal sense, to indicate a geographical or spatial direction: Abram offers Lot to choose a direction (Genesis 13:9), and King David asks the woman from Tekoa if there is anything "to the right or to the left" of her words (2 Samuel 14:19), meaning nothing added or omitted. It is also found to describe the use of the right hand in battle (1 Chronicles 12:2). Finally, it takes on a sense of command or military orientation in Ezekiel (21:21), where the sword is commanded to turn in all directions.
H3231.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of direction and choice in life: choosing between left and right is choosing one's path. For the Christian, it evokes the biblical idea that the right side is associated with blessing and protection (as when God places His elect at His right hand), while the straight path requires a conscious orientation of one's life towards God.

sens: firstborn son of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel
descendants of Jimna, called Jimnites
H3232G.detail:
1. Jimna is the firstborn son of Asher, one of Jacob's twelve sons. He first appears in the list of Asher's children during the descent into Egypt (Genesis 46:17), and then in the census in the wilderness (Numbers 26:44). His name means "right hand" in Hebrew, a probable allusion to strength or preeminence.
2. The descendants of Jimna are referred to as "Jimnites" and formed a distinct branch of the tribe of Asher. In the second census (Numbers 26:44), they are listed as a separate family, alongside the other descendants of Asher.
H3232G.origine: The name Jimna literally means "right hand" (yamin = hand, right). This root is common in biblical Hebrew, where the "right hand" often symbolizes strength, authority, or blessing. The name reflects Jimna's importance as the firstborn son of Asher.
H3232G.emploi: Jimna is mentioned three times in the Bible, always as the son of Asher. He appears in the account of the descent into Egypt (Genesis 46:17), where Jacob brings his entire family to meet Pharaoh. The same name and his descendants reappear in the census lists of the wilderness (Numbers 26:44 and 1 Chronicles 7:30), which enumerate the families of Israel after the Exodus. These passages show that Jimna's lineage has continued through the generations, forming a stable branch of the tribe of Asher.

sens: Levite assisting the high priest Hezekiah during the temple reforms
H3232H.detail: Jimna is a Levite who participated in the major religious reforms led by King Hezekiah in the 8th century BCE. His son Kore was a gatekeeper of the temple and responsible for distributing the voluntary offerings presented to God. Both worked towards restoring worship according to the Law of Moses.
H3232H.origine: The name means "right hand" in Hebrew, possibly evoking blessing or strength. It is the same name as one of Asher's sons mentioned in the Old Testament, but the biblical uses here refer to a Levite from the time of the divided monarchy, several generations later.
H3232H.emploi: Jimna appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 31:14, in the midst of the account of the temple reforms under King Hezekiah. He is mentioned as the father of Kore, a Levite who kept the eastern gate of the temple and managed the offerings made to the Lord. This role shows that Jimna's family had an important responsibility in the functioning of worship.

sens: Located on the right side of the body (the side opposite to the left)
The right hand, or right arm
The right foot
Figuratively: that which is in accordance with justice, with the order established by God
H3233G.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the right direction, the right side of the human or animal body, in opposition to the left side. In Exodus 29:20, blood is placed on "the right ear" of Aaron and his sons at the time of their consecration as priests.
2. It particularly applies to the right hand, considered the hand of strength and action. In Leviticus 14:16, the priest dips "the finger of his right hand" in oil to sprinkle and purify.
3. Similarly, it designates the right foot, marking the laterality of the body. Purification rituals mention the big toe of the right foot (Leviticus 14:14).
4. In a broader usage, the word can mean "right" in a moral or legal sense — that which is in accordance with justice and the will of God — although this figurative use is less frequent in our references.
H3233G.origine: The Hebrew word יְמָנִי (yemaní) comes from the root יָמִין (yamín), which properly designates the right hand or the right side. This root is attested in many Semitic languages and refers to a universal observation: among most humans, the right hand is the dominant hand. The right side is associated in biblical thought with strength, favor, and honor, while the left often symbolizes weakness or malice. A derivative of the same root (יְמָנִי in the sense of "south") also exists, as in biblical Hebrew the south was the right side when facing east.
H3233G.emploi: This word appears about ten times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the books of Leviticus and in the laws of ritual purity. It is used very concretely to designate the body parts that receive the blood of consecration or the oil of purification: the right ear, the right hand, the right foot. These rituals, repeated in Exodus 29, Leviticus 8, and Leviticus 14, show that the right side of the body had symbolic importance in Israel's worship. The word also appears in a historical context in Ezekiel 4:6, where the prophet must lie on his right side. The usage remains always spatial and concrete, never purely abstract in our references.
H3233G.portee: This word reminds us that biblical worship engages the entire body of the believer, not just the spirit. The choice of the right side — associated with strength and honor — shows that consecration to God involves the totality of our person, including our faculties and our most powerful actions. Learning the deep meaning of these ritual gestures helps us understand how Israel viewed the relationship between body, action, and holiness before God.

sens: Located on the right, on the right side of the body or a place
The right hand, or what belongs to the right hand
The southern side, when looking east
H3233H.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what is located on the right, in opposition to the left. In the temple of Jerusalem, one column was placed "on the right" and the other "on the left" of the portico (1 Kings 7:21). Similarly, when the king was protected by his guards, they positioned themselves "from the right side to the left side of the house" (2 Kings 11:11).
2. The word also specifically refers to the right hand or what relates to it. Among the Hebrews, the right hand symbolizes strength, blessing, and power.
3. In geographical orientation, "right" designates the south. When looking east (the main direction in biblical geography), the right is south; the Segond translates as: "He placed the sea on the right side, to the southeast" (2 Chronicles 4:10).
H3233H.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that expresses the idea of "right" or "rightness." In biblical Hebrew, as in many languages, the term for "right" (right hand) has extended to spatial orientation, as the right was the natural reference point when facing east. The right hand, stronger and more commonly active, also symbolizes power and divine favor.
H3233H.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in architectural descriptions of the temple of Jerusalem and its protection. It is found in the books of Kings and Chronicles, which recount the construction and life of the temple, as well as in Ezekiel, who describes a vision of the future temple. The meaning changes little: it is always about locating something or someone by specifying that it is "on the right." In 2 Chronicles 4:10, the translation "southeast" shows that the context of direction prevails: it specifies where the sea (great bronze basin) was placed in the courtyard of the temple.
H3233H.portee: This word reminds us that the right, in the Bible, is never neutral: it evokes strength, blessing, and divine favor. When we pray, when we speak of the right hand of God, we speak of His active and benevolent power.
