Although this word is mainly technical and descriptive, it grounds us in the concrete and spatial reality of the temple, the place where God dwelled among His people.

sens: man of the tribe of Asher
son of Helem
brother of Tzophach, Shalesh, and Amal
H3234.detail: Jimna is a man belonging to the tribe of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. He is a son of Helem, mentioned as a leader or representative of his tribe during the time of the divided monarchy (after the death of Solomon). He is cited alongside his brothers Tzophach, Shalesh, and Amal in the genealogy of the sons of Helem in 1 Chronicles 7:35.
H3234.origine: The name Jimna literally means "He will hold" or "He will retain," formed from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of holding back or restriction. It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries a reference to God, suggesting a trust in the divine power to contain or control circumstances.
H3234.emploi: Jimna appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:35, in the genealogical record of the tribe of Asher. It is a simple lineage mention, situating this man in the genealogical tree of Asher and confirming his role as a family or tribal leader at a time when genealogies served to establish the identity and territorial rights of the tribes in Israel.

sens: To give one thing and receive another in return
To replace something with something else
To boast about, to take pride in
H3235.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is commercial or material exchange: giving one thing and receiving another in return. It is bartering, commerce where each gives something to obtain an equivalent.
2. By extension, it means to replace, substitute: to abandon something to take another in its place. In Jeremiah 2:11, the people "change their glory," meaning they replace it, abandon it for another.
3. In a context of pride or reputation, the word can mean to boast about, to take pride in, to glorify. In Isaiah 61:6, the people "will glorify the glory" of the nations, meaning they will derive honor and pride from it.
H3235.origine: The verb comes from a root that evokes the idea of replacement and permutation. The word belongs to the family of terms related to exchange and transformation. The basic image is that of two things changing places: one gives one to receive the other.
H3235.emploi: The word appears only twice in the provided Bible. In Isaiah 61:6, it expresses the future pride of the people: they will glorify the wealth and splendor of the nations. In Jeremiah 2:11, it describes the sin of the people: Israel has exchanged its true glory (the Lord) for worthless gods. These two uses show how the people can either abuse this right of exchange (sin) or enjoy it rightly (future promise).
H3235.portee: This word reminds the believer of the cost of spiritual exchange: Israel has "changed" its living God for mute idols. It is a call not to make the same ruinous trade — not to abandon the true glory of God for worthless substitutes. The promise in Isaiah invites us to await the day when the faithful will be able to glory, not in material wealth, but in their restored relationship with God.

sens: Man of the tribe of Asher during the time of the divided monarchy
H3236.detail: Jimra is a man of the tribe of Asher, son of Tzophach. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:36, in the genealogy of the descendants of Asher. He was a family leader within his tribe.
H3236.origine: The name Jimra means "bitterness" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of bitterness or harshness. It is a typical personal name from the ancient Semitic world.
H3236.emploi: Jimra appears only once in the biblical texts, in 1 Chronicles 7:36. He is listed in the genealogical record of the sons of Tzophach, a member of the tribe of Asher. This genealogy enumerates the main families of the tribe during the period of the divided monarchy in Israel. His name is preserved to show the family structure and lineages of this tribe.

sens: To exercise brutal or unjust domination over someone, causing harm through violence or abuse of power
To deceive someone in business, to harm them through lies or fraud
To mistreat, to act harshly towards a weak or defenseless person
H3238.detail:
1. To oppress means to remove someone's rights by force or abuse of authority. It is to reduce someone to powerlessness, to deliberately cause them harm. In Ezekiel 18:7, the one who "does not oppress anyone" is described as just: this is someone who does not take advantage of their position to do harm. The word evokes the image of a force that crushes, of power used against the weak.
2. To deceive here means to cheat someone or to swindle them in a transaction. Leviticus 25:17 clearly forbids this: "None of you shall oppress his neighbor." It is a type of soft violence, that of fraud or dishonesty in business.
3. To mistreat means to act harshly towards someone, to treat them without respect or consideration. Exodus 22:21 forbids to "mistreat" the foreigner; Ezekiel 22:7 reproaches for having "mistreated the foreigner." The emphasis here is on the absence of compassion and justice towards the most vulnerable.
H3238.origine: The root יָנָה reveals the idea of pressing, of constraining someone against their will. In biblical Hebrew, the verb is mainly used in the simple form (Qal) or in the causative (Hiphil), emphasizing an action of domination or mistreatment. The word always expresses an unjust relationship of force between a powerful and a weak person.
H3238.emploi: This verb appears about 20 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the laws of Moses (Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy) and in the oracles of the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel). In the Law, it forbids oppressing the foreigner, the poor, or the debtor, which shows that biblical justice protects the vulnerable. In the prophets, the word describes the sins of the powerful: Jeremiah 22:3 commands the king not to oppress, while Ezekiel 22:29 accuses the men of the people of oppressing and committing robbery. The context is always one of morality and social justice.
H3238.portee: This word reminds the reader that God defends the small and the weak. The Law of Israel was revolutionary for its time in forbidding oppression and deceit towards the poor and the foreigners. To oppress is to forget that God sees everything and that He will be the judge. For the Christian, this word calls for vigilance against any form of abuse of power, fraud, or lack of compassion, and to follow the example of Him who humbled Himself to lift up the oppressed.

sens: City in northern Galilee, in Upper Galilee, in the territory of Naphtali
H3239A.detail: Janoach is a locality in northern Israel, located in Upper Galilee in the territory assigned to the tribe of Naphtali. It was conquered and depopulated by the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser during his military expedition in Palestine around 733-732 B.C., as reported in the account of 2 Kings 15:29.
H3239A.origine: The name Janoach means "He rests" in Hebrew, composed of the element ya (a form of the divine name) and the verb noach (to rest). This place name reflects a divine proclamation or trust in divine protection, typical of city names in the land of Israel.
H3239A.emploi: Janoach appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 15:29. It is listed among the cities of the Northern Kingdom conquered by Tiglath-Pileser during his invasion of Galilee. The text mentions Janoach alongside other significant localities such as Ijjon, Abel-Beth-Maaca, and Kedesh, highlighting the extent of the devastation suffered by the Northern Kingdom of Israel.

sens: Locality at the border of the territory of Ephraim
Landmark in the delineation of the border between Ephraim and Manasseh
H3239B.detail:
1. Janoach is a city or site located at the border of the territory of the tribe of Ephraim. It served as an important geographical landmark for delineating the lands given to this tribe after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 16:6).
2. The place is mentioned in the precise description of the border between Ephraim and Manasseh: the boundary "went eastward to Janoach," and from there "it went down to Atharoth and Naarath" (Joshua 16:7). It was one of the landmarks that allowed for the accurate tracing of the land divisions between the tribes.
H3239B.origine: The name Janoach literally means "He rests." It is a site whose precise location in Canaan is not definitively identified today, but whose name evokes rest or the stable establishment of the people of Israel in the territory given by God.
H3239B.emploi: Janoach is mentioned twice in the Bible, both times in the book of Joshua (chapters 16:6 and 16:7), in the passage that describes the division of territory among the tribes of Israel after the conquest. The text is very precise: it lists a series of localities and waterways to trace the exact borders of each territory. Janoach is included as a cardinal point of the border between Ephraim and Manasseh, located toward the east.

sens: Mountain city in the territory of Judah
H3241.detail: Janum is a small city located in the mountains of Judah, not far from Hebron. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of cities that Joshua distributes to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of the land (Joshua 15:53).
H3241.origine: The name Janum literally means "asleep" or "that sleeps," although the significance of the place name is likely symbolic or metaphorical — perhaps evoking a calm and secluded place in the mountains.
H3241.emploi: Janum appears only once in the Scriptures, in Joshua 15:53, in the context of the division of the territory of Canaan. It is listed among the mountainous cities of southern Judah, between Beth-Tappuah and Aphekah, indicating that it was a locality of some administrative importance even though it played no major role in later biblical narratives.

sens: young shoot or tender branch of a tree
a branch that rises or develops
figuratively: a descendant, a lineage that prospers
H3242.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a young shoot or tender branch that comes from the trunk or root — something alive and flexible, capable of growth. In Ezekiel 17:4, the eagle "takes the highest of its branches": this refers to a main and vigorous branch, the one that grows upward.
2. The branch is therefore a branch that rises, that elevates — the very image of growth and life that ascends toward the sky.
3. By extension, the branch can symbolize a lineage or a descendant that continues and prospers, as a new branch is the living extension of the tree from which it comes.
H3242.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of sucking or nourishing, then that of growing and developing. This root suggests a movement of life that pushes and nourishes. The word aligns with the symbolism of the branch in the Old Testament: a green branch is always a sign of life and divine blessing.
H3242.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 17:4, in a parable about two eagles and a cedar. The eagle "takes the highest of its branches," meaning the highest and most vigorous branch of the great cedar that represents the people of Judah. This action marks the historical intervention of a foreign power that removes the elite of the people and deports them. The political and symbolic context is that of the Babylonian exile.
H3242.portee: This word reminds us that the people of God are like a tree that God cares for: its branches, its children and descendants, are under His watch and governance. Even the removal of a branch does not escape God's plan. For the believer, it is a call to recognize oneself as a branch of the Lord's vine, dependent on and alive from His sap.

sens: Nocturnal bird with tufts (small feathers) on its head, classified among unclean animals
Symbol of desolation and ruin in prophecies
H3244.detail:
1. It is a nocturnal bird characterized by small feathers standing up on its head, known as tufts. The Law of Moses classifies it among the unclean birds that should not be eaten (Leviticus 11:17 and Deuteronomy 14:16), like the screech owl and the swan.
2. In prophecies, the owl becomes the image of a destroyed and abandoned land: it inhabits ruins because it loves deserted and silent places. When Isaiah announces the desolation of Edom, he mentions the owl alongside the pelican and the raven to paint a picture of total desolation (Isaiah 34:11).
H3244.origine: The Hebrew word yanshûph likely comes from a root expressing the gaze or the piercing cry characteristic of this bird. It is a distinctive nocturnal bird of the ancient Near East, well known to the Israelites for its mournful calls and its presence in abandoned places.
H3244.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate a specific bird. The first two occurrences (Leviticus and Deuteronomy) are found in lists of unclean animals that the Israelites should not consume: it is a cultic and dietary prescription. The third occurrence (Isaiah 34:11) moves from the dietary context to that of prophecy: the owl becomes the poetic symbol of a ruined and abandoned land. In this apocalyptic passage, the bird reminds that God will judge those who oppose Him.
H3244.portee: This word invites the reader to discover how the Bible uses nature to speak of divine justice: a simple bird becomes the sign of a world shaken by judgment. It also reminds that holiness manifests itself in the concrete details of daily life, even in food choices. The nocturnal owl symbolizes the moral and spiritual darkness that follows the abandonment of God.

sens: Lay the foundations of a building, a city, or a work
Establish, institute, set up in a durable way
Create, install in order and solidity
H3245.detail:
1. To lay the foundations of a building, a city, or a work: the word first evokes the concrete act of digging, preparing, and setting the base stones upon which everything else rises. When Solomon built the temple, the Bible notes that he laid the foundations carefully (2 Chronicles 3:3). It conveys the idea of solid, durable, well-anchored in the ground.
2. To establish, institute, set up in a durable way: the word extends beyond construction to denote the action of organizing, creating a system or order that will endure over time. King Ahasuerus thus orders his house to drink according to everyone's desire (Esther 1:8) — he establishes a stable regulation. It conveys the idea of a decision that takes root and lasts.
3. To create, install in order and solidity: in the broadest and deepest sense, the word applies to the creative action itself. God founded the world and all that it contains (Psalms 89:12), He established the earth on its foundations (Psalms 104:5). It is the divine act that lays the groundwork for all reality, creating with wisdom and certainty.
H3245.origine: The Hebrew root יסד (y-s-d) expresses the primary idea of placing something firmly, setting it solidly. It is related to the notion of base, foundation, that which does not move. The noun "foundation" or "foundations" (יסוד, yesod) comes directly from this root and designates the stones or earth that support a construction. In Hebrew, the image is always that of the base, the solid that supports everything else.
H3245.emploi: The verb יסד appears 42 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms, Isaiah, and the accounts of the temple's construction. It is first used in a concrete sense for the foundations of buildings (the temple by Solomon in 2 Chronicles 3:3, the walls of Jerusalem by Zerubbabel in Zechariah 4:9). It extends to the sense of establishing cities (Isaiah 14:32: God has founded Zion) or ordinances (Esther 1:8). But its most frequent and exalted use concerns God: He has founded heaven and earth, He has established the world on its immutable foundations (Psalms 89:12, 104:5). The word always carries with it the idea of solidity, durability, and creative order.
H3245.portee: This word speaks to the believer of stability: that which God alone guarantees to all created things, and that which He offers to those who place their trust in Him. When the Bible affirms that God has "founded" the earth or that He "founds" Zion, it assures that divine order holds, that it will not collapse. It is a word of anchoring and trust in the heart of the world's uncertainty.

sens: The starting point or origin of something
The solid base on which a construction rests
What is established or instituted
H3246.detail:
1. The foundation is primarily the starting point, the origin of an action or a period: in Ezra 7:9, it refers to the beginning of the journey ("on the first day of the first month was the beginning of the journey"), the moment when Ezra and his companions set out from Babylon.

2. It is also, in the literal sense, the base of a construction: the stones laid first so that everything else stands. This is the central image of the word: without a foundation, nothing can be solid or durable.

3. More broadly, it is what is established or instituted — the base on which a decision, a law, an institution is built. The foundation is what gives stability and meaning to everything that rises above it.
H3246.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to lay foundations" or "to establish." It evokes the act of the builder who lays the first stones: it is a gesture of creation and order. The root suggests the idea of establishing something in a stable and durable way, by placing it on a solid base.
H3246.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 7:9, where it designates the beginning of Ezra's journey from Babylon to Jerusalem: "On the first day of the first month was the beginning of the journey." It is a temporal usage, where foundation means the starting point of an action. Although rare in the biblical text, this word belongs to the rich family of Hebrew terms related to stability, construction, and order — central themes in the Bible.
H3246.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of a solid foundation in the Christian life: whether for our faith, our decisions, or our relationships, everything rests on a foundation. The Bible emphasizes the foundation that God establishes (Isaiah 28:16 speaks of a foundation stone laid in Zion). It is an invitation to examine what our choices and trust rest upon.

sens: Base, substructure on which a construction rests
In a figurative sense: what serves as a base or starting point for something
H3247G.detail:
1. The word first designates the material foundation of a building, the solid base dug into the ground on which the walls are built. It is the support that gives stability to the entire structure.
2. In a figurative sense, it represents what founds, supports, or establishes something durably — a principle, an institution, a truth. Like the foundation of a building, it must be solid for everything else to hold.
H3247G.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to establish" or "to lay down." It evokes the action of founding, digging, and laying the bases. This idea is found in several Hebrew words of the same family that speak of structure, stability, and establishment.
H3247G.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 23:5, where it designates the "Gate of the Foundation" of the temple in Jerusalem — probably one of the gates of this edifice whose name reminded that it was built on a solid foundation. The usage shows that the word applies to concrete and architectural realities.
H3247G.portee: The word reminds us that a construction, whether material or spiritual, needs solid foundations. For the believer, this invites reflection on what constitutes the true bases of their faith and life.

sens: The foot or base of a structure, that on which it rests
The base or principle on which something immaterial rests
What is durable and stable over time
The origin or deep roots of something
H3247H.detail:
1. The foot or base of a structure, that on which it rests: in the sacrifices of Leviticus, the blood is poured at the "foot of the altar" (Leviticus 4:25), that is, at its base, on the ground where it rests. This is the concrete and spatial sense: the lower part that supports.
2. The base or principle on which something immaterial rests: in Proverbs 10:25, the righteous possess "everlasting foundations," which means that their life and existence rest on unshakeable principles, while the wicked are swept away like dust.
3. What is durable and stable over time: the "foundations" become an image of solidity and permanence. When Ezekiel announces that the foundations of Egypt will be overthrown (Ezekiel 30:4), he prophesies the total and lasting collapse of its power.
4. The origin or deep roots of something: in Job 4:19, men "derive their origin from dust" — the word describes these primal roots, what a thing proceeds from and is made of at its deepest level.
H3247H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to found" or "to establish firmly." It is related to verbs that express the action of laying a foundation or giving a base to something. The starting image is physical: the foot or base on which a building rests. From there, the word naturally shifts to the figurative sense of principle, origin, or moral and spiritual stability.
H3247H.emploi: The word appears 18 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the legislative and prophetic books. In Leviticus (at least 7 occurrences: 4:7, 4:18, 4:25, 4:30, 4:34, 5:9, 8:15, 9:9), it always designates the foot of the altar, the place where the blood of the sacrifice accumulates — this is the concrete and priestly sense. In the wisdom and prophetic books (Job, Proverbs, Ezekiel, Micah, Habakkuk), the word rises to the figurative sense: the stability of a life (Proverbs 10:25), the fragility of man (Job 4:19), the ruin of powers (Ezekiel 30:4). The word thus plays on a tension: the physical and visible foundation becomes the image of spiritual or moral realities, stable or threatened depending on whether one obeys God or not.
H3247H.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on what they are building their life upon. Like the righteous in Proverbs 10:25, is it on everlasting foundations — that is, on God, His word, His faithfulness — or on shifting sand? The sacrificial usages remind us that the foundation of our access to God comes through the gift of blood and atonement. The word thus calls for examination: do our choices, our values, our hopes rest on solid ground or on emptiness?

sens: The act of founding, establishing a city or a building solidly
Base, foundation on which a structure rests
Figuratively: what serves as a stable base for a community or a work
H3248.detail: 1. It is primarily the act of founding a city, constructing it by placing it solidly. Psalm 87 uses it this way: the city of Zion is "founded on the holy mountains" (Psalms 87:1), which means it is built, established in a stable and lasting way on these heights. 2. By extension, the word designates the foundation itself, the support point, the solid base on which a construction rests. 3. Spiritually, this image of solidity and stability applies to the position of Zion as the city of the living God: it is well established, unshakeable, because God has placed it on a sure foundation.
H3248.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of placing something in a stable and lasting manner. This root evokes the image of the mason or builder who drives the foundations into solid ground so that the building stands for a long time.
H3248.emploi: The word appears only once in the preserved Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 87:1. It is used to express that Zion is "founded" on the holy mountains. This rarity of the term in Hebrew contrasts with the importance of the concept of foundation and stability throughout Scripture: other more common Hebrew words (like מוסָד) carry the same meaning. Its unique usage gives particular weight to this assertion about the solidity of Zion.
H3248.portee: This word reminds us that God's holy city is not built randomly or on sand, but on an unshakeable base: the mountains of His holiness. It is an assurance for the believer: what God founds stands firm. The image inspires confidence in the face of changes and threats.

sens: a person who reproves someone for their faults
one who convinces by words
H3250.detail:
1. This word designates a person who reproves another, who convinces them of their wrongs or errors. It is one who is not afraid to say to someone: "you have acted wrongly." In Job 39:35, it is used for one who would dare to contest God Himself, who would claim to refute or correct Him — an image of the absurd contrast between the human and the Almighty.
2. More broadly, it is one who judges and convinces by words, who exposes faults. The word carries the idea of a moral authority that challenges.
H3250.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root ysûr (יסור) which literally means "to turn," "to remove" — the image of turning someone away from their wrong path. The noun thus designates one who does this work of warning and correction. It is a rare word in the Hebrew Bible, formed to express this specific role of one who reproves or disputes with someone.
H3250.emploi: The word appears only once in the provided biblical text: in Job 39:35, at the heart of God's discourse to Job. God poses rhetorical questions about who would dare to contest or refute Him — "the one who contends with God, does he have a reply?" The context shows God affirming His superhuman power and wisdom, and describing the absurdity of a human pretending to play the role of one who reproves the Creator. The word underscores the enormity of such a claim.
H3250.portee: This word invites reflection on humility: no human has the authority to reprove God or correct Him. But it also implicitly states that reproving is part of language and life — we reprove those we love or esteem. The real question is: who has the right to do so? Before God, the only posture is listening and obedience.

sens: woman of the patriarchal era, daughter of Haran
H3252.detail: Jisca is a woman mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 11:29. She was the daughter of Haran and the sister of Lot and Milca. Her Hebrew name means "she who looks" or "she who sees afar," which evokes a keen vision. She lived during the time of Abraham, when the patriarchal families were dispersing and seeking wives.
H3252.origine: The name Jisca comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to look" or "to see." It is a feminine name that suggests someone endowed with vision or insight. Although the name is rare and appears only once in the preserved biblical texts, it fits within the tradition of Hebrew names that describe a notable quality or action.
H3252.emploi: Jisca is mentioned only once in Genesis 11:29, in the genealogical list presenting the women of the patriarchs Abram and Nahor. She is listed as the daughter of Haran and sister of Milca (who will marry Nahor) and Lot (the nephew of Abraham). This genealogical passage situates the family ties of the early patriarchs and shows how the descendants of Terah settled and formed unions.

sens: A Levite during the reign of King Hezekiah
Officer in charge of overseeing the offerings at the temple
H3253.detail: Jismakia is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi, dedicated to the service of the temple and assisting the priests. He lived during the reign of King Hezekiah (8th century BC), during the period of the divided monarchy in Israel and Judah. Jismakia was one of the officials responsible for overseeing the offerings and gifts brought to the temple in Jerusalem during the great religious reform led by Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 31:13). He worked under the direction of Conaniah and his brother Shimei, as well as under the authority of the king and Azariah, the chief of the house of God. His role was important in the administration of worship and the management of the temple's resources.
H3253.origine: The name Jismakia means "Jehovah sustains". It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God (Jah or Yah, a shortened form of the Tetragrammaton). This type of name was common in Israel and expressed trust in God's protection and blessing. The name reflects the family's faith in divine support.
H3253.emploi: Jismakia appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 31:13. He is mentioned as one of ten Levites responsible for overseeing the offerings and gifts at the temple in Jerusalem during the religious reform led by King Hezekiah. These men were tasked with receiving, controlling, and distributing the contributions intended for divine worship. His historical existence attests to the administrative organization of the temple and the seriousness with which the righteous kings of Judah conducted their religious reforms.

sens: Increase a quantity by adding something more
Perform an action again, restart
Continue without interruption
Join someone or something, attach to
Accumulate, intensify (notably blows or punishments)
H3254G.detail:
1. To add means to increase a set by putting something more in it: Eve gave birth "again" to her brother Abel (Genesis 4:2), meaning she added a child to Cain. It simply means to increase the number or quantity.
2. The word also expresses the repetition of an action already done: a war that "continues" (1 Samuel 19:8) is an action that adds to what has happened before, that reproduces. It means to do again.
3. To continue means to add time to an ongoing action, prolonging it without finishing. The war persists because each day more combat is added.
4. In the passive form, the word means to be incorporated into a group or person: someone joins a people or community. It becomes an additional element of a whole.
5. Finally, to add punishments or blows means to accumulate them, to intensify: God strikes "seven times more" according to sins (Leviticus 26:21), meaning He increases the severity of judgment by adding plagues.
H3254G.origine: The verb יָסַף (yasaph) comes from a root that evokes the idea of increasing or adding. The family of the word includes terms that speak of addition and accumulation. In biblical Hebrew, this verb is very productive and is often used with a second verb to indicate repetition: "add to do" means "do again." This construction reveals how Hebrew thinks about repetition: not as a simple iteration, but as the addition of a new action.
H3254G.emploi: The verb יָסַף appears 119 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the simple past and present forms. It is found in almost all historical and poetic books. Genesis uses it for numerical addition (children born successively) and the repetition of action. In the laws (Leviticus, Deuteronomy), it intensifies punishments: "strike seven times more." The books of Samuel and Kings use it to describe the continuation of war or relationships. Esther uses it to speak again to the king. Job uses it to introduce a new word. The word can also express the impossibility of continuing: "does not rise again" (Isaiah 24:20). Its meaning varies according to the context and the type of object to which one adds: object, person, action, or abstraction (sin, repentance).
H3254G.portee: This verb expresses human repetition, inevitable and often guilty. When Israel "adds" to doing evil after the death of Ehud (Judges 4:1), it is a return to the cycle of sin. The word also reveals God's patience: He "adds" increasing punishments, giving His people the chance to understand. For the believer, this verb invites reflection: what do we add to our lives? Are we doing "again" good, or falling back into evil? It is a call to constancy in good, to faithfulness that does not cease.

sens: To put something extra, to increase the quantity
To repeat an action, to do it again
To intensify, to gradually strengthen
To join someone, to form a union
To increase the severity of a punishment or a threat
To provide, to supply abundantly
H3254H.detail:
1. Ajouter means to put one thing in addition to another to increase the quantity. This is the most concrete action of the word: one adds a fifth to the price of a redeemed tithe (Leviticus 27:31), or Abraham takes another wife, meaning he adds one to his first wife (Genesis 25:1).
2. To repeat an action or to do it again: this is to add once more the same act. When Genesis 37:5 and 37:8 speak of making or recounting a dream "again," it means to continue the previous action.
3. To intensify or gradually strengthen: the basic action is doubled to become stronger. Saul fears "more and more" David (1 Samuel 18:29), meaning his fear grows continuously. Likewise, the righteous "grows stronger and stronger" (Job 17:9).
4. To join someone or to join a group: this means to add oneself to a community to form a union. This usage reflects the idea of increase applied to human relationships.
5. To increase the severity of a punishment, a threat, or vengeance: to strike with more force and intensity. Jezebel threatens Elijah by saying, "May the gods deal with me ever so severely" (1 Kings 19:2), meaning she calls upon herself a maximum punishment if she does not kill him.
6. To provide or supply abundantly: the enrichment that comes from continuous addition. "Wealth brings many friends" (Proverbs 19:4), meaning it continually adds new friends.
H3254H.origine: The Hebrew root ysp (יסף) expresses the fundamental idea of adding, joining one thing to another. It generates several forms that nuance this basic meaning: the simple "to add" (Qal), "to join oneself" or "to be joined" (Niphal), and "to cause to be added" or "to increase further" (Hiphil). The word belongs to an ancient Semitic family and is found in other related languages. In Hebrew, this root is very productive and runs through all the books of the Bible.
H3254H.emploi: The verb ysp appears 89 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the historical, wisdom, and legislative books. In the Law (Pentateuch), it refers to the addition of offered portions or fifths during compensation (Leviticus 27:31). In historical narratives, it describes both concrete actions (taking an additional wife) and emotional or gradual intensifications (growing fear, increasing strength). In the Psalms and Proverbs, it acquires a spiritual dimension: asking God to add years, wisdom, or blessing. The context determines the nuance: the addition can be positive (increasing wealth or joy) or negative (multiplying blows or hardships).
H3254H.portee: This verb teaches that life is built through addition: each action, each decision adds to the previous ones and grows progressively. For the believer, it invites asking God to add His blessings, His wisdom, His years of life, rather than His punishments. It also reminds of the heart's responsibility: what we add to our words or actions shapes our character and destiny. It is a word of hope and warning at the same time.

sens: to increase in quantity, number, or intensity
to become larger, more important, to strengthen
H3255.detail:
1. Accroître means to add to what already exists, to grow in quantity or strength. In Daniel 4:36, King Nebuchadnezzar recounts that his power "only increased": he speaks of his dominion that was amplifying, expanding, becoming more formidable as his royal authority was restored. It is the image of something that grows, that accumulates progressively.
2. In a figurative sense, accroître can describe the strengthening or extension of an immaterial reality: power, glory, magnificence, or splendor, as in the same verse where all these attributes of the king are added and multiplied together.
H3255.origine: The Hebrew verb יסף (yasaph) comes from a root expressing the idea of adding, of adding on. The family of this word includes terms related to accumulation and increase. In biblical Hebrew, this verb is common to describe what is added or multiplied, and it evokes the concrete image of piling up, adding one thing to another.
H3255.emploi: The verb יסף appears only once in this passage from the book of Daniel (4:36), a text written in late Aramaic. Nebuchadnezzar describes here the moment when, after his restoration, all the elements of his royalty return to him and amplify: his reason, his glory, his kingdom, his magnificence, his splendor. The context shows an accumulation of blessings and strengths that mutually reinforce each other, until his power itself experiences continuous growth.
H3255.portee: This verse reminds us that power and glory are only lasting if they are linked to reason and wisdom. After his humiliation, the king recognizes that his power increases, but only when his reason has been restored to him: it is a lesson on the importance of righteousness and submission to divine will for true prosperity.

sens: To punish or correct someone through blows or suffering
To correct, to set someone right by pointing out their faults
To instruct, to teach someone through experience and trials
In a figurative sense: the trial that educates and strengthens faith
H3256.detail:
1. Châtier primarily means to physically punish, to correct through punishment: this is the most direct sense. God punishes Israel by striking it with plagues for its sins (Leviticus 26:18), and the punishment aims to bring the people back to obedience. This is also what a master may inflict on a servant or an authority on a guilty person (Deuteronomy 22:18).
2. Châtier also means to correct, to set right by pointing out the fault: this is moral correction that calls for change. God corrects Israel so that it understands its errors and abandons them, like a father corrects his son (Jeremiah 30:11: "I will chasten you with justice," says the Lord, who does not abandon His people despite everything).
3. Châtier also means to instruct, to teach through experience and correction: one who has received instruction can in turn instruct others (Job 4:3: "You have often instructed others").
4. On a deeper level, God's punishment is a form of spiritual education: the trials He sends strengthen faith and teach the believer to walk in righteousness (Psalms 118:18: "The Lord has chastened me, but He has not given me over to death").
H3256.origine: The Hebrew verb יָסַר comes from a root that evokes the idea of warning, correcting, setting right. The same root produces the noun מוּסָר (mûsâr), which means instruction, correction, or discipline. This word frequently appears in Proverbs to describe the teaching that shapes character. In Hebrew, to châtier is never a mere blind punishment: it is always an act of love aimed at correcting and forming.
H3256.emploi: The verb יָסַר appears 38 times in the Old Testament. It is very common in Proverbs, where it speaks of the importance of correcting a child (Proverbs 29:17, 19); in the Psalms, where the faithful asks the Lord to instruct him (Psalms 94:10, 12); and in historical narratives, where God punishes kings or peoples to turn them away from their sins (Deuteronomy 8:5: "Know that the Lord your God chastens you as a man chastens his son"). The word slightly changes nuance depending on the context: it can be an immediate and local correction, or a spiritual trial that educates in the long term. Jeremiah especially emphasizes this: God chastens Israel in exile, not to destroy it, but to bring it back to repentance (Jeremiah 30:11; 31:18).
H3256.portee: For the Christian, this word teaches that God's trials and corrections are not marks of rejection, but signs of His paternal love. As the epistle to the Hebrews writes (quoting Proverbs), "whom the Lord loves, He chastens." Understanding that God chastens is therefore an invitation not to lose heart in the face of difficulties, but to see it as an opportunity to learn and grow in faith. It is also a call to correct others with mercy and firmness, for their good, not for their destruction.

sens: Tool used to remove and transport the ashes from the altar
H3257.detail: 1. A shovel is a service utensil of the sanctuary, intended to remove the ashes that accumulate under the altar of burnt offerings. It is a practical and necessary instrument to keep the place of worship clean (Exodus 27:3). It is part of the complete equipment of the altar, alongside forks, ash pans, and braziers, all made of polished bronze to withstand fire and weather (1 Kings 7:40, 7:45).
H3257.origine: The Hebrew word יָע comes from a root that evokes the action of removing or sweeping. It is a very ancient term designating a simple but indispensable tool for the work of the temple. The word belongs to the concrete vocabulary of sacrificial worship in the Old Testament, with no common equivalent in everyday secular vocabulary.
H3257.emploi: The word appears nine times in the Bible, almost always in connection with the construction or maintenance of the Tabernacle and the Temple. It is first encountered in the instructions for the Tabernacle (Exodus 27 and 38), then in the organization of the transport of sacred objects (Numbers 4:14). It later appears in the accounts of the construction of Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 7:40, 7:45; 2 Chronicles 4:11, 4:16). Finally, it is mentioned during the destruction of the Temple by the Babylonians, when the ash pans and shovels are taken as plunder (2 Kings 25:14; Jeremiah 52:18). The consistency of this term shows that it is a stable and recognized liturgical object.
H3257.portee: The shovel reminds us that worship rendered to God requires order, cleanliness, and material organization. This simple, often forgotten utensil represents piety in the details: God cares that everything is done well, even in the removal of ashes. It invites the reader to see that each object of worship has a function and dignity, and that serving God involves the body and the gestures of daily life.

sens: City of Judah, probably near Bethlehem
H3258G.detail: Jabez is a city located in Judah, apparently in the region of Bethlehem. It is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 2:55 as the residence of families of scribes. The name etymologically means "sorrow" or "pain," but Jabez itself is primarily known as a center of scribes and writers in ancient Israel.
H3258G.origine: The name Jabez comes from a Hebrew root meaning "sorrow" or "pain." It is a place name, probably given to the city for its symbolic or historical significance. The biblical text designates it primarily by its function: a place inhabited by families of scribes, that is, professionals of writing and the transmission of texts.
H3258G.emploi: Jabez appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:55. It is presented there as the residence of several families of scribes: the Tiriteans, the Shimeathites, and the Sucathites. These families are identified as descendants of the Kenites, a people linked to Hamath, the father of the house of Rechab. The mention of Jabez in this genealogical context shows the importance of this city as a center of intellectual and religious activity in Judah.

sens: A man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the Divided Monarchy
The chief of a family of Calebites
A city of Judah near Bethlehem
H3258H.detail:
1. Jabez is a character from the tribe of Judah mentioned for the first time in 1 Chronicles 4:9. His name literally means "sorrow" in Hebrew, as his mother named him so in remembrance of the pain of his childbirth — a name that recalled his difficult entry into the world.

2. He was the chief of a family of Calebites, that is, a lineage belonging to the clan of Caleb within Judah. The text distinguishes him by saying that he "was more honorable than his brothers," indicating that he held some importance among his kin (1 Chronicles 4:9).

3. Jabez is also mentioned as the name of a city of Judah, apparently located near Bethlehem. This is probably the place where this character lived or from where his family came.
H3258H.origine: The Hebrew name יַעְבֵּץ comes from a root that evokes pain and sorrow. Its etymology remains linked to the physical experience of suffering during childbirth: this is exactly what his mother expressed by naming him so. The name carries with it the memory of a painful moment, transformed into personal identity.
H3258H.emploi: Jabez appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles 4, in verses 9 and 10. The first account (4:9) explains the origin of his name: his mother named him "Jabez" because she bore him in pain. The second (4:10) shows Jabez invoking the God of Israel with a specific prayer: he asks God to bless him, to enlarge his territory, to be with him, and to keep him from harm and suffering. The text concludes that "God granted what he requested," making Jabez a biblical example of answered prayer.
H3258H.portee: The story of Jabez teaches the reader that God listens to sincere prayer, even when it comes from someone whose name bears the mark of suffering. It reminds us that our painful past does not define our destiny: Jabez, called "sorrow" by his mother, was able to experience God's blessing. It is an encouragement for anyone seeking to overcome difficult circumstances by turning to the Lord with confidence.

sens: To set or establish something decisively
To designate or assign a charge or function to someone
To meet at a fixed place or time
To gather together, especially by calling or summoning
To conclude an agreement or commitment (especially a marriage)
H3259.detail:
1. To set or establish something: to give it a stable and definitive form. In Exodus 21:8, a master establishes his intention to marry his slave; in Exodus 25:22 and 29:43, God sets a meeting place, establishing a regular appointment with His people.
2. To designate someone for a task or responsibility: to entrust it to a person or assign it to them. In Numbers 10:3, Moses designates those who are to summon the assembly.
3. To meet at an appointment: two or more people come together at a scheduled time. In Exodus 29:43, God says He will meet with Israel at the sanctuary; in Amos 3:3, the prophet asks if two can walk together without having agreed to meet.
4. To gather, summon to assemble a group: to call people together to gather. In 2 Chronicles 5:6, King Solomon summons the assembly of Israel for the service of the sanctuary; in Numbers 10:4, the sound of the trumpet gathers the princes.
5. To agree, to consult to act in common accord: to forge a bond or project together. In Psalms 48:5, the kings conspired against Jerusalem.
H3259.origine: The Hebrew verb יָעַד comes from a root meaning "to set" or "to establish," with the fundamental idea of giving something a stable form. The basic image is that of placing or firmly setting. This verb is used for any act that creates a relationship or a determined moment: setting a date, establishing an appointment, designating a person. It is a word that the Bible regularly uses when speaking of order, commitment, and organized meeting.
H3259.emploi: This verb appears 29 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the narratives of law (Exodus, Numbers), history (Kings, Chronicles), and the Psalms. It describes both everyday acts and divine acts. When God is the subject, it means setting an appointment ("I will meet with you"), establishing an order or a place (the sanctuary, the ark). When it refers to humans, the verb speaks of voluntary gathering (princes coming together), official summoning (gathering the assembly), or agreement between parties (kings consulting together). The context oscillates between order (someone establishing something) and meeting (two parties finding themselves together), but the key idea remains: there exists a fixed, desired, established point of convergence.
H3259.portee: This word shows that God leaves nothing to chance: He establishes places, moments, appointments to meet His people. This reveals His desire for a stable and organized relationship. For the reader, it emphasizes the importance of presenting oneself at the time and place He has set, and the honor represented by the fact that He "meets" with us. It is also a call to order and responsibility: when an authority "summons," it is so that all may assemble seriously.

sens: prophet and seer of Israel during the time of the divided monarchy
H3260.detail: Jeedo is an Israelite prophet mentioned only once in the Bible, in the last verse of the account of King Solomon's reign. He is referred to as "the prophet to Jeroboam, son of Nebat" (2 Chronicles 9:29), which means he proclaimed God's words to Jeroboam, king of the Northern Kingdom. His name means "appointed" or "established by God," reflecting his prophetic vocation.
H3260.origine: The name Jeedo comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to fix" or "to establish." It is a variant or another form of the name Iddo (עִדּוֹ), which also designates a prophet. The meaning of the name "appointed" evokes someone whom God has specially designated for a mission, which corresponds to the vocation of prophets.
H3260.emploi: Jeedo appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 9:29, where he is named among the documentary sources of Solomon's acts. He is described as a "prophet" (nabi in Hebrew) and a seer who announced God's words to Jeroboam, king of northern Israel after the kingdom's division. This brief mention suggests that he was known to the author of Chronicles as a respected prophetic authority of his time.

sens: To sweep away, completely remove something by driving it out.
Figuratively, to destroy or annihilate something in one sweep, like an irresistible force.
H3261.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of sweeping or removing things with a broad gesture: one clears away, drives far off what is in one's path. In Isaiah 28:17, hail "carries away" the refuge of falsehood — it destroys and removes it violently.
2. Figuratively, it means to completely annihilate: divine justice carries away lies and false supports like a broom sweeps away dust. It is the image of a force that cannot be held back, which destroys everything in an instant.
H3261.origine: The Hebrew verb יָעָה (ya'ah) expresses the rapid and powerful movement of sweeping or removal. Its root evokes the idea of driving away, casting far from oneself. The word belongs to the family of verbs of violent action: it is to sweep away with force, which is why it applies to irresistible divine judgments.
H3261.emploi: The word appears only once in the provided biblical text: in Isaiah 28:17. The prophet announces God's judgment against the people's false refuges — their lies and idols. Hail, a weapon of divine judgment, "carries away" what seemed solid. This choice of verb emphasizes the irresistibility of judgment: nothing can stop God's justice; it sweeps everything in its path.
H3261.portee: This word reminds us that false refuges — the lies on which one builds one's life, the false securities — cannot withstand God. It invites the believer not to rely on what is false, but on divine justice and truth, which alone endure.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of exile and return
H3262.detail: Jeuel is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from exile. He is presented as the son of Zerah and a leader among the Judeans who returned to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 9:6). He and his brothers, numbering six hundred ninety, represent an important family among those who reoccupied the holy city after the Babylonian captivity.
H3262.origine: The name Jeuel literally means "God sweeps away" or "God carries away." It is composed of the divine name El (God) and a verb that evokes the action of sweeping or removing. This name reflects a trust in divine action, either to purify or to carry away. It is a typical name of the post-exilic period, when Judean families reaffirmed their identity and relationship with God after the trials of captivity.
H3262.emploi: Jeuel appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 9:6, in the genealogical list of families that resettled in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is designated as the son of Zerah and the leader of a large family of Judeans (six hundred ninety members). This mention is part of the official record of Judah's restoration, highlighting the importance of the elders who led the people in rebuilding community and religious life.

sens: Son of Shaharaim and Hodesh, member of the tribe of Benjamin
H3263.detail: Jeuts is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, living during the time of the divided monarchy. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:10, where he is presented as the son of Shaharaim and Hodesh, and as a family leader alongside his brothers Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, and others.
H3263.origine: The name Jeuts literally means "counselor" in Hebrew, formed from the root that designates counsel or advice. It is a theophoric or functional name that reflected the esteem given to the one who bore it in the Benjaminite society of his time.
H3263.emploi: Jeuts appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 8:10. This passage lists the descendants of Benjamin and establishes the genealogies of the family leaders of this tribe. Jeuts is listed among the children of Shaharaim and Hodesh, alongside brothers, some of whom are also heads of households. This genealogical context is typical of the lists in the book of Chronicles, which reconstructs the history of Israel by emphasizing lineages and tribal organization after the exile.

sens: father of Elhanan, warrior during the united kingdom of Israel
H3265.detail: Jair is the father of Elhanan, one of David's valiant warriors. His son is famous for having killed Lachmi, the brother of Goliath, during a battle against the Philistines (1 Chronicles 20:5). The name "Jair" means "he enlightens" or "forest," evoking clarity and strength. Although he is mentioned little in biblical history, his fame comes from his son and the military exploits of his family in service to King David.
H3265.origine: The name Jair comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to illuminate" or "to shine," and can also evoke the idea of "forest." It is a fitting warrior name for a man of David's time, reflecting the values of strength and clarity. In the text of 1 Chronicles, Jair is also known as "Jaare-oregim" (יַעֲרֵי אֹרְגִים), which literally means "forests of weavers," perhaps a description of the place of origin of his family.
H3265.emploi: Jair is mentioned only once in the Bible: in 1 Chronicles 20:5, as the father of Elhanan. This mention appears in the context of David's valiant warriors and battles against the Philistines. The parallel in 2 Samuel 21:19 also designates him as "Jaare-oregim." His only known historical role is being the father of a military hero.

sens: Son of Esau and Oholibamah, Edomite chief during the Patriarchs' era
H3266G.detail: Jeush is one of the sons that Esau had with his wife Oholibamah, daughter of Anah. He is first mentioned in Genesis 36:5 as one of the three sons born to Esau in the land of Canaan. The text designates him as a chief among the Edomites (Genesis 36:18), showing that he held a position of authority in his community, alongside his brothers Jaalam and Korah.
H3266G.origine: The name Jeush (or Jeush) means "He hurries to aid," suggesting a prompt and helpful personality. The name belongs to the lineage of Esau, ancestor of the Edomites, and appears in genealogical lists tracing the leaders of the neighboring peoples of Israel.
H3266G.emploi: Jeush is mentioned four times in Scripture, exclusively in the genealogical lists of Esau. He first appears in Genesis 36, where the Segond names him "Jeush" in verses 5 and 14, then "chief Jeush" in verse 18, which emphasizes his status as a chief of the Edomite clan. He is also cited in 1 Chronicles 1:35 in the parallel genealogical account of Esau's sons. These four occurrences confirm his role as a minor historical figure but rooted in the Edomite lineage.

sens: Son of Bilhan, of the tribe of Benjamin
Member of Saul's family through his ancestor Eshek
Gershonite Levite of the house of Shimei
H3266H.detail: Jeusch is a name borne by at least three men in the Old Testament. The Jeusch mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:10 is the son of Bilhan, himself the son of Jediael, of the tribe of Benjamin. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy, surrounded by his Benjaminite brothers, Ehud, Kenaana, Zethan, Tarsis, and Achishachar. The other Jeuschs mentioned elsewhere in Scripture include a distant descendant of King Saul (through Eshek) and a Gershonite Levite of the house of Shimei, but the latter appears only once in the genealogies.
H3266H.origine: The name Jeusch means "He hastens to help" or "One who hastens to aid," formed from a Hebrew root expressing quick assistance and protection. It is a theophoric name that reflects trust in God as the one who quickly comes to the aid of His people.
H3266H.emploi: Jeusch appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:10, where he is listed among the sons of Bilhan, son of Jediael, of the tribe of Benjamin. It is in a genealogical context, within the lists of descendants of the patriarchs and tribes of Israel that the author of Chronicles compiles to preserve the memory of the families of Israel. The name is not associated with any particular event or action, but its presence in these genealogies shows its importance for the tribe of Benjamin and for the continuity of the people.

sens: Son of Eshek, descendant of Saul
Levite of the house of Shimei
H3266I.detail:
1. Jeusch is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:39. He is the son of Eshek and the brother of Ulam and Eliphelet. He belongs to the long genealogy of the descendants of King Saul, which connects him to the royal house of Israel.
2. The name Jeusch also refers to a Levite of the house of Shimei, part of the tribe of Levites designated for temple service. This second occurrence shows that the name was borne by different men in ancient Israel.
H3266I.origine: The name Jeusch (in Hebrew יְעוּשׁ) literally means "He hastens to help" or "He runs to aid." It reflects the biblical idea that God or a man who has received His help comes promptly to assist. This type of theophoric name (containing a divine reference) was common among the Hebrews to express trust or prayer towards the Lord.
H3266I.emploi: Jeusch appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:39, where he is presented as the son of Eshek and the brother of Ulam and Eliphelet. This mention is part of a genealogy of Benjamin that traces back to the descendants of King Saul. The text does not report any particular event concerning Jeusch; he simply appears in the genealogical record of the Benjamite families, making him a figure of ancient Israel's history that remains discreet.

sens: Son of Shimei, Levite of the family of Gershon
H3266J.detail: 1. Jeusch is a Levite of the tribe of Levi, a member of the family of Gershon (one of the three main families of Levi). He is the son of Shimei and the brother of Jahath, Zina, and Beria. He lived during the time of the wilderness wanderings and the kingdom of Israel. He is first mentioned in the Bible in 1 Chronicles 23:10, in the list of the sons of Shimei who served in the temple.
H3266J.origine: The name Jeusch literally means "He hastens to help" or "He hastens to aid." It is a theophoric name, composed of Hebrew elements that express the idea of quick and effective help from God.
H3266J.emploi: Jeusch appears twice in Scripture, only in 1 Chronicles 23:10-11. These two verses are part of the list that King David established of all the Levites and their functions in the temple. Jeusch is counted among the descendants of Shimei. The text specifies that Jeusch and his brother Beria, having few sons, formed together one paternal house in the census. This indicates their administrative and cultic role at the time of organizing the temple service.

sens: Son of King Rehoboam and Mahalath
Prince of the kingdom of Judah during the divided monarchy
H3266K.detail: Jeusch is a son of King Rehoboam of Judah and his wife Mahalath. He appears in the list of the king's children enumerated in 2 Chronicles 11:19, where he is cited among the sons that Mahalath bore to Rehoboam: "She bore him sons: Jeusch, Shemariah, and Zaham." As a king's son, Jeusch was a prince of the kingdom of Judah during the divided monarchy, after the schism that separated the kingdom into two during the time of Rehoboam.
H3266K.origine: The name Jeusch literally means "He hastens to help" or "He hastens to aid," formed from a root that evokes the idea of rushing, coming quickly to help. It is a theophoric name, meaning it expresses a characteristic attributed to God, the one who hastens to come to the aid of His people. This type of name was common in the royal families of Israel and Judah.
H3266K.emploi: Jeusch appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 11:19. He is mentioned as one of the three sons that Queen Mahalath bore to King Rehoboam (along with his brothers Shemariah and Zaham). Rehoboam married several women and had many children who strengthened his dynasty at the beginning of his reign over Judah. Beyond this simple genealogical mention, the Bible provides no further information about Jeusch or his deeds.
H3266K.portee: The mention of Jeusch reminds us that even great biblical figures — like King Rehoboam — are situated within concrete family lineages. It invites us to see how God guided the royal dynasties of His people, and how the names of these children, bearing spiritual meanings, reflected the hopes and values of the believers of Israel.

sens: Who has audacity, who acts without fear and restraint
Who is violent, impetuous in his manner or gestures
Who is fierce, unyielding, uncivil
H3267.detail: 1. This word primarily evokes one who acts without fear, with a somewhat excessive boldness, without holding back. The "audacious" people of Isaiah 33:19 are an aggressive and unreserved people. 2. Audacity can also take on a violent and impetuous character: one who does not hesitate to strike, to advance in a brutal manner. It is a force without gentleness. 3. The term even describes a barbaric and fierce behavior, uncouth, unyielding — which corresponds to the translation "barbarian" in the verse of Isaiah where this people with an obscure language appears as rough, almost savage in their manner of being.
H3267.origine: The Hebrew word יָעַז (ya'az) belongs to a small family of Hebrew terms expressing strength and hardness. Its primitive root would evoke a brutal energy, unrefined. The fundamental meaning oscillates between "to be strong" and "to be fierce": it is strength when it manifests itself in a raw, aggressive manner, without civility.
H3267.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 33:19, in its participial form ("the one who is audacious"). It describes the invading people that Judah will no longer see triumph: a violent people, with an unintelligible language, a barbaric tongue. The context shows that it is less a moral audacity than a brutality, a warlike ferocity. The word emphasizes not only courage or impudence but the brutal, savage, uncultured aspect of the conquering people.
H3267.portee: This word reminds God's people that the apparent strength and audacity of enemies will not last: they will be defeated. It also teaches that human audacity, when devoid of fear of God and civility, is nothing but sterile brutality. For the believer, it is a comfort: the noisy and arrogant power of the world does not have the final word.

sens: Levite musician in the service of King David
Man made courageous by God
H3268.detail: Jaaziel is a Levite whom King David appointed to participate in the musical service before the Ark of the Covenant in Jerusalem. His name literally means "made courageous by God" or "God has made me courageous": it expresses how God gives courage and boldness to those He calls to serve Him. He first appears in the Scriptures in 1 Chronicles 15:18, among the musicians and singers gathered by David for this great solemn procession.
H3268.origine: The name Jaaziel means "God has made courageous" or "God has made me bold". It is composed of two elements: "ya'az" which means "to be strong, to be courageous, to dare", and "el" which means "God". This same Jaaziel is also called Aziel (a shorter form of the same name) in 1 Chronicles 15:20, showing how Hebrew personal names could have multiple forms in biblical lists.
H3268.emploi: Jaaziel appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 15:18. He is presented as one of the Levites of the second order chosen by David to form the group of musicians who would accompany the Ark of the Covenant during its transfer to Jerusalem. He appears in an impressive list of musicians and gatekeepers, all mobilized for what was considered a major solemn and religious occasion of David's reign. Although we only have this single mention, it shows his importance in the organization of worship during the time of the Davidic monarchy.
H3268.portee: Jaaziel reminds us that God chooses people to serve Him and gives them the courage necessary to fulfill this mission. His name, which means "God has made me courageous", encourages us to see that serving God is not a matter of personal strength, but of the courage that God grants to those He calls.

sens: Levite of the lineage of Merari, mentioned in the register of priestly families during David's time
H3269.detail: 1. Jaazija is a Levite belonging to the family of Merari, one of the three main branches of the Levites (along with Kohath and Gershon). He appears in the genealogical census of the Levitical families drawn up during David's reign to organize the temple service. According to 1 Chronicles 24:26, he is the son of Merari, and according to 1 Chronicles 24:27, his own sons — Shoham, Zaccur, and Ibri — are listed in the same register, indicating that he was an important link in this priestly genealogy.
H3269.origine: The name Jaazija means "made courageous by the Lord" or "he whom the Lord has made bold". It is composed of the Hebrew root עָזַז (ʿazaz), which means "to be strong" or "to strengthen", and the divine name Yah. This type of theophoric name, which contains the name of God, was common among the Levites and expressed the relationship between the bearer and the Lord.
H3269.emploi: Jaazija is mentioned twice in 1 Chronicles 24, at the heart of the register of Merari's families. In 1 Chronicles 24:26, he is listed as a direct son of Merari alongside Machli and Mushi. In 1 Chronicles 24:27, his own descendants are detailed: his four sons — Shoham, Zaccur, Ibri, and Beno — are listed to establish their right to Levitical service. These passages show that Jaazija was considered an ancestral figure within the Levites, charged with a specific cultic responsibility in the organization of the temple in Jerusalem.

sens: Fortified city of Gilead, east of the Jordan, in the territory of Gad
H3270G.detail: Jaezer is a city formerly occupied by the Amorites, then conquered by the Israelites during their entry into Canaan (Numbers 21:32). It was located east of the Jordan, in the region of Gilead, and belonged to the tribal territory of Gad (Joshua 13:25). The Levites also had a presence there, as it was one of the cities assigned to the descendants of Hebron (1 Chronicles 26:31). It was a prosperous city, famous for its vineyards: the prophet Isaiah speaks of it with emotion when he laments the destruction that will come upon it (Isaiah 16:9).
H3270G.origine: The name literally means "he has helped" or "God helps", making it a common theophoric name in Israel. The city retained this name since ancient times, even before the Israelite conquest. Its exact location remains debated, but it was situated within the geography of the Transjordan plateau.
H3270G.emploi: Jaezer appears twelve times in the Bible, mainly in the accounts of conquest and land distribution (Numbers and Joshua), where it is listed among the cities that the Israelites captured. It is mentioned again during David's census (2 Samuel 24:5), where it serves as an important geographical landmark. The Chronicles place it among the Levitical cities (1 Chronicles 6:81; 26:31). The prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah mention it in the context of judgment on Moab, revealing its economic and cultural significance in this border region.

sens: Levitical city east of the Jordan, in Gilead, territory of Gad
H3270H.detail: Jaezer is a city that belongs to the Levites, located in Gilead, a mountainous region east of the Jordan, in the territory assigned to the tribe of Gad. It was once an Amorite city before coming under Israelite control. Its name means "God has helped". In the only biblical occurrence preserved, the prophet Jeremiah weeps over it and the surrounding vineyard region, devastated by invaders (Jeremiah 48:32).
H3270H.origine: The name Jaezer comes from Hebrew and literally means "God has helped" (from the root concerning divine help). It is a historical place in the biblical world, known for its fertile vineyards and its economic importance in the Transjordan region.
H3270H.emploi: Jaezer appears only once in the Segond 1910, in Jeremiah 48:32, where it is mentioned alongside Sibmah, another vineyard region. The prophet weeps over these fertile lands now devastated by God's judgment against Moab. This mention situates Jaezer as a prosperous agricultural center, particularly renowned for its vineyards extending to the Dead Sea.

sens: To clothe someone with a garment or protective layer
Figuratively, to envelop with protection or spiritual dignity
H3271.detail:
1. To cover means here to clothe someone with a garment, as one dresses someone in clothes. In Isaiah 61:10, the prophet describes how God "covers him with the robe of salvation": the image is that of a garment that envelops, protects, and gives a new appearance — just as a bridegroom adorns himself with a diadem for his wedding, in the same way the believer is adorned by God with the garments of salvation.
2. Figuratively, to cover means to envelop with protection or glory. It is not just a material garment, but a spiritual transformation: God clothes the believer with a new identity, that of salvation and deliverance. It is an image of restored dignity and divine protection.
H3271.origine: The verb יָעַט (ya'at) belongs to the family of Hebrew words expressing the action of covering or enveloping. The basic image is that of a covering that completely envelops, hence the meaning of to clothe or to dress. The word evokes the idea of protection and transformation through clothing.
H3271.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 61:10. It is used in a context of restoration and messianic joy: the prophet announces that God clothes the believer with the garments of salvation and the robe of deliverance. This passage belongs to the section of comfort in the book of Isaiah, where God promises a complete and glorious transformation to His people. The use of the verb "to cover" reinforces the idea that this restoration is total and enveloping.
H3271.portee: For the Christian reader, this verse teaches that salvation is not merely a technical pardon, but a true transformation: God "clothes" the believer with a new identity in Christ. The image of the garment emphasizes that this righteousness is not one's own, but is given, clothed, enveloping. It is an invitation to understand salvation as a restored dignity and complete divine protection.

sens: to give advice, a recommendation
to consult, deliberate together
H3272A.detail:
1. To give advice or a recommendation to someone: this is the role of one who guides through wisdom or experience. In Daniel 6:7, the magistrates and satraps come to "counsel" King Darius, proposing a decree that benefits them.
2. To consult, to deliberate together to make a decision: several people exchange their opinions in order to reach a common resolution. This conveys the idea of gathering to reflect and determine the best course of action.
H3272A.origine: This Aramaic word is the counterpart of the Hebrew verb יָעַץ (ya.ats), which means "to counsel" or "to give advice." The root evokes the idea of weighing a question, forming a judgment. In Hebrew, this verb appears notably when speaking of seeking counsel from someone wise. The Aramaic y.at is a variant, marking the continuity of meaning across the two languages of the biblical text.
H3272A.emploi: The word appears only once in biblical Aramaic, in the account of Daniel during the time of Darius. The high officials come to "counsel" the king regarding an edict, depicting a form of political deliberation — here tinged with calculation, since their counsel aims at their own interests. This context shows that "to counsel" is not a neutral act: the advice can be wise or self-serving, sincere or manipulative. The word emphasizes the importance of carefully choosing those from whom we receive advice.
H3272A.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites vigilance: where do our counsels come from? And from whom do we seek wisdom? The Bible reminds us that true counsel comes from the Lord, not from men driven by self-interest or cunning. Receiving counsel requires discernment.

sens: One who gives advice, who counsels
One who assists an authority to help make decisions
One who participates in the deliberations of a court or administration
H3272B.detail:
1. A counselor is a person who gives advice, who helps someone think and decide. This is someone experienced and trustworthy whose opinion is sought before taking action.

2. In an official context, a counselor is a collaborator who assists an important authority (a king, an emperor) by giving their opinion on government affairs. The king of the land from which Ezra comes charges him with inspecting the lands and bringing gifts to the temple: this royal envoy takes with him the decisions of the king "and his counselors" (Ezra 7:14-15), meaning his entire administration.

3. The counselor can also be a member of a consultative assembly, someone whose opinion matters in important decisions of a court or kingdom.
H3272B.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root יָעַץ (*ya.ats*), which literally means "to counsel" or "to give advice." The form used here is a participle, meaning it designates the person who performs this action: a counselor is "one who counsels." This root expresses the idea of deliberation and common reflection to guide a decision.
H3272B.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible, only in Ezra 7. It refers to the high counselors of the king of Persia (Artaxerxes) who accompany Ezra's mission. In verses 14 and 15, we see that the king acts "and his counselors": the royal authority consults its close counselors before deciding. These counselors are not named individually, but they form an official council around the monarch. The context shows that a counselor is an influential person, capable of participating in the major decisions of the kingdom, such as sending an official mission and granting significant gifts.
H3272B.portee: This word reminds us that wisdom comes from mutual counsel and reflection. A counselor is someone who helps make good decisions by bringing their experience and discernment. For the Christian, this illustrates the importance of listening to wise opinions before acting and not acting alone in significant matters. It is also an image of trust: one entrusts their affairs to those whose prudence and integrity are recognized.

sens: Reubenite chief during the divided monarchy
Son of Adonikam who returned from exile with Ezra
Merarite Levite, gatekeeper of the tabernacle and musician
Chief of the Levites under King Josiah
Son of Hotkham, warrior of David
Ancestor of Gibeon
H3273G.detail:
1. Jeiel is primarily a chief of the clan of Reuben, mentioned in genealogies as "the first" of his brothers (1 Chronicles 5:7). He represents an important lineage of the northern tribe during the period when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah coexisted.
2. Under King Ezra, one of the descendants of this name returns from exile with a group of repatriates, showing how the name has been passed down through generations.
3. Another Jeiel served as a Levite in the temple: he kept the gates of the tabernacle and played the harp and psaltery in worship before the ark, thus participating in the liturgical service.
4. Under the reign of Josiah, a Jeiel held a position of responsibility among the Levitical leaders, attesting to his spiritual influence.
5. A valiant warrior of David bore this name, son of Hotkham the Aroerite, integrated into the royal military elite.
6. A Jeiel is also mentioned as a man of Gibeon and ancestor of King Saul, linking his lineage to the first royal dynasty of Israel.
H3273G.origine: The name Jeiel (יְעִיאֵל) literally means "God sweeps away" or "God carries away" (from יָעָה "to sweep away, to carry off"). It expresses the idea that the Lord removes or purifies, a powerful image related to divine judgment or deliverance. This name, borne by several notable men in Israel, reflects a theological conviction: that God controls destinies and purges what needs to be purged.
H3273G.emploi: Jeiel is the name of at least ten different men in the Scriptures, all mentioned in the Chronicles and the accounts of Ezra-Nehemiah. The earliest historically is the Reubenite chief of 1 Chronicles 5:7, living at the time of the division of the kingdoms. Other Jeiels appear after the Babylonian exile (Ezra), serving as Levites, temple musicians, religious leaders, and warriors of David. This recurrence of the name suggests that it carried honor and distinction in Israelite families, particularly among the Levites and the military elite. The different contexts in which the name appears (genealogies, worship, Levitical ministries, royal service) show that its bearers enjoyed a recognized place in the community of Israel, both in the north and the south.

sens: Elite warrior in the service of King David
Son of chief Hotham
H3273H.detail:
1. Jehiel is a powerful warrior among David's valiant men. He is one of the elite warriors whose names are listed among the conquerors and heroes of the king (1 Chronicles 11:44).
2. He is the son of Hotham the Aroerite and the brother of Shama. These two brothers fought together in the service of King David and are mentioned together among the military heroes of that time.
H3273H.origine: The name Jehiel (or Jeiel) means "God sweeps away" or "God carries away" — composed of the divine name El (God) and a root evoking the action of sweeping or removing. This name expresses confidence in the powerful action of God. Several men bore this name in the history of Israel, at different periods: sons of exiles who returned with Ezra, Levites, leaders of the people.
H3273H.emploi: Jehiel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:44, where he appears alongside his brother Shama in the list of the "thirty-seven valiant men" of David — the elite warriors who formed the core of the royal army. This appearance in this famous list highlights his trusted role with the king and his military importance. At this time of the monarchy established under David, these warriors represented the martial elite of the kingdom.
H3273H.portee: The presence of Jehiel among David's valiant men reminds us that the king's success relied on faithful and courageous men. For the Christian reader, this account illustrates the importance of loyalty and courage in the service of the Lord and His plans — not by strength alone, but by strength put to the service of justice and the order desired by God.

sens: Levite musician during the time of David, bearer of harp and psaltery
H3273I.detail: Jeïel is a Levite who served under King David as a musician and gatekeeper of the tabernacle.
