In 1 Chronicles 15:18-21, he is listed among the musicians tasked with accompanying the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem, playing the eight-stringed harp. In 1 Chronicles 16:5, he is again mentioned among the chief musicians under the direction of Asaph, with stringed instruments. He was a servant of worship, responsible for both sacred music and guarding the entrance of the sanctuary.
H3273I.origine: The name Jeïel (יְעִיאֵל in Hebrew) means "God sweeps away" or "God removes," composed of the divine element El (God) and a root evoking the action of removing or purifying. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing a divine action. There is a variant of the same name, Yékhiyya (Jehiah), which refers to the same person in 1 Chronicles 15:24.
H3273I.emploi: Jeïel is mentioned three times in 1 Chronicles, always in connection with the musical service and the guarding of the tabernacle during King David's time. Along with Asaph and other Levite musicians, he participated in the solemn worship ceremonies, notably in the transportation of the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. These mentions show that the liturgical service of the temple required both musical skill (harp, psaltery) and responsibilities as a guardian. Jeïel represents those anonymous servants of worship whose memory has been preserved in Scripture.

sens: Levite of the lineage of Asaph during the time of King Jehoshaphat
H3273J.detail: Jeïel is an ancestor of Jahaziel, the Levite who, filled with the Spirit of the Lord, brings a word of comfort to Jehoshaphat and Judah threatened by an enemy coalition (2 Chronicles 20:14).
H3273J.origine: The name Jeïel (or Jehiel) means "God sweeps away" or "God carries off," formed from the Hebrew elements for God and a root evoking the action of sweeping or scattering. This name fits within the Hebrew tradition of theophoric names—composed with the name of God—that recall divine action.
H3273J.emploi: Jeïel appears only once in the Segond 1910, in 2 Chronicles 20:14, as a direct ancestor of the prophet Jahaziel. He is mentioned in the context of the genealogy of the Levite who delivered a decisive divine word to King Jehoshaphat during a political and military crisis. This genealogical placement emphasizes his belonging to the lineage of the Asaphite Levites, musicians and prophets of the temple.
H3273J.portee: The mention of Jeïel shows that God places His words in the mouths of those who come from faithful lineages. The name of the God who "sweeps away" (that is, who judges and purifies) in the context of a prophecy of deliverance reminds us that God acts beyond any external threat to protect His people.

sens: Man living during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel
H3273K.detail: Jeïel is a biblical character mentioned only once in the Bible. He was the secretary of King Uzziah (also called Ozias) and was responsible for keeping the records of the royal army. In 2 Chronicles 26:11, we learn that he worked alongside the commissioner Maaséja to count and enumerate the soldiers who formed the various bands of the king's army, which was then placed under the command of Hanania, one of the king's chiefs. His role was therefore administrative and important in the military organization of the kingdom.
H3273K.origine: The name Jeïel literally means "God sweeps away" or "God carries off" (from the Hebrew root יע, evoking the action of sweeping or removing, and אל, which denotes God). This name expresses trust in divine action. Several men bear this name in Scripture, but this one is distinguished by his specific function with King Uzziah in the 8th century BC.
H3273K.emploi: Jeïel appears only once in the Old Testament, in 2 Chronicles 26:11. He is presented there as the secretary (or scribe) of King Uzziah, responsible for keeping the records of the army of the kingdom of Judah. His name appears alongside that of Maaséja, the commissioner, and both worked together to account for the soldiers and document their organization into different military bands. This unique mention shows the importance of scribes in the administration of biblical kingdoms, even though we know of this Jeïel only through this single documented function.

sens: Character from the time of the divided monarchy, chief Levite during the reign of King Jehoshaphat
H3273L.detail: Jeïel is a man of the people of Israel mentioned only once in the Bible, during the time when the kingdoms of Judah and Israel coexisted. In 2 Chronicles 29:13, he appears as one of the chief Levites mobilized during the great religious reform led by King Jehoshaphat: he is part of the descendants of Asaph who participate in the purification of the temple and the restoration of divine worship. His role was to organize the liturgical service and music in the temple.
H3273L.origine: The name Jeïel means "God sweeps away" or "God removes," composed of the Hebrew roots denoting God (El) and the action of sweeping or removing. Several characters bear this name or a variant (Jehiel) in the Old Testament, illustrating its common usage among the people of Israel.
H3273L.emploi: Jeïel is cited only once in Scripture, in 2 Chronicles 29:13. He is mentioned there as one of the sons of Asaph, a great lineage of musicians and prophets of the temple. His appearance in this historical passage shows the importance of the role of the Levites in public worship: they were not only servants of the sanctuary but also men responsible for the spiritual leadership of the nation during religious reforms.

sens: Levite character during the reign of King Josiah
Chief Levite responsible for providing for the Passover sacrifice
H3273M.detail: Jeïel is a Levite who lived during the time of King Josiah in Judah. In 2 Chronicles 35:9, he is mentioned as one of the chief Levites (along with his brothers Conania and Schemaeja) who generously contributed to the Passover sacrifices by providing the other Levites with five thousand lambs and five hundred oxen for the celebration. His name means "God sweeps away" or "God carries off"—an image of divine purification and judgment.
H3273M.origine: The name Jeïel comes from the Hebrew יְעִיאֵל, composed of two elements: "Yah" or "Yé" (the Lord) and "iël" (God), with a root evoking the action of sweeping or removing. This type of theophoric name (which bears the name of God) was common among the Levites, expressing trust in divine action. Several characters bear this name in the Chronicles and in the accounts of Ezra, all linked to the service of the temple or to the community restored after the exile.
H3273M.emploi: Jeïel appears only once in the Bible in 2 Chronicles 35:9, where he is designated as chief of the Levites during the time of Josiah. On this occasion, he is among the leaders who provided the animals for the Passover sacrifice, which shows his status as a leader in the temple's cultic service. The Chronicle mentions him alongside his brothers Conania and Schemaeja, highlighting his importance in organizing religious services and his generosity towards the cultic community.
H3273M.portee: The figure of Jeïel reminds the reader of the essential role of the Levites in Israel's worship and their commitment to providing for the needs of the temple. His generous act—giving abundantly for the Passover—illustrates how serving God requires not only responsibilities but also an offering of oneself and one's possessions. It is a silent yet concrete example of faithfulness in divine service.

sens: Son of Adonikam who returned from exile with Ezra
H3273N.detail: Jeïel is a man whose name means "God sweeps" in Hebrew. He appears in the account of the return from exile: he is one of the sons of Adonikam who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:13). His name in the Hebrew text is יְעִיאֵל (Yeïel), sometimes a variant of Jehiel. The mention of Jeïel in the list of returnees highlights the importance given to this massive return of the Jewish people after the Babylonian captivity: every name matters in this story of restoration.
H3273N.origine: The name יְעִיאֵל (Yeïel) literally means "God sweeps" or "God removes." It is formed from the root y‛l (to remove, to sweep) and the word אל (El, God). This type of theophoric name — containing the divine name — was common among the Hebrews: it expresses God's action in the person's life. Several people bore this name at different periods in Israel's history.
H3273N.emploi: Jeïel is mentioned only once in the Bible in Ezra 8:13, in the list of returnees who came back from Babylon with Ezra around 458 B.C. He is noted as one of the last three sons of Adonikam, a family leader whose group included sixty men. This appearance in the official record of the return underscores his status as a household leader and his role in the reconstruction of the Jewish community after the exile. The text does not provide further details about his life or functions.

sens: A man of the tribe of Nebo who returned from exile with Ezra
An ancient figure borne by several characters in the Old Testament
H3273O.detail: 1. Jeïel is one of the sons of Nebo mentioned in the list of men who had taken foreign wives during the exile in Babylon. Ezra 10:43 names him among those who had to repudiate these wives to uphold the Law (Ezra 10:43). His name appears at the return of the people to the promised land, in the context of religious renewal under Ezra. 2. The name "Jeïel" (or Jehiel) has designated several important characters throughout Israel's history: Levites responsible for the service of the tabernacle and the temple, warriors in the service of kings David, Josiah, and Uzziah, and ancestors of King Saul. It is a name borne by men of responsibility and service in the community.
H3273O.origine: The name Jeïel means "God sweeps" or "God carries away." It comes from the Hebrew root that evokes the action of sweeping or removing something. It is a theophoric name — containing the name of God — that expresses trust in divine action. Several variants like Jehiel are attested in the biblical text.
H3273O.emploi: Jeïel is mentioned only once in the Segond in Ezra 10:43, where he is listed among the descendants of Nebo who acknowledged their wrongdoing in taking foreign wives and agreed to repudiate them. This mention is part of the movement of religious restoration and separation from neighboring peoples that characterized the return from exile. The name Jeïel appears elsewhere in the Old Testament to designate other men in Israel's history, but this entry concerns only the character from Ezra 10:43.
H3273O.portee: The account in Ezra 10 shows how, upon returning from exile, the people had to make difficult choices to remain faithful to God's Law. Jeïel, though not well-known, embodies this willingness to break with compromise and return to holiness. His story reminds the reader that repentance and obedience to God sometimes require personal sacrifices, but they pave the way for blessing and restoration.

sens: Ancestor of King Saul, father of Gibeon
Head of a Benjaminite family during the united monarchy
Name also borne by several other characters in the Old Testament
H3273P.detail:
1. Jeïel is primarily known as the father of Gibeon, a distant ancestor of King Saul. The Bible mentions him in 1 Chronicles 9:35 as a man of the tribe of Benjamin who lived in Gibeon with his wife Maacah, and who had many sons including Kish, the father of Saul.
2. The name Jeïel (or Jehiel in some variants) was borne by several other important men in Israel's history: heads of Levitical families, warriors of David, a scribe of King Uzziah, and other prominent figures in the Levitical and royal lineage.
H3273P.origine: The name Jeïel literally means "God sweeps" (from the Hebrew root meaning "to sweep" or "to clean"). It is a theophoric name — that is, it carries the name of God — and expresses the idea that God has an action of purification or judgment. This type of name was common in Israel to express faith in divine action.
H3273P.emploi: Jeïel is a personal name borne by several different men in the Old Testament. The Jeïel mentioned in 1 Chronicles 9:35 is that of Gibeon, a genealogical ancestor of King Saul. Other namesakes held important positions: some were Levites serving in worship, others were warriors or royal officials. The Bible uses this name to mark the importance of these family lineages in the religious and political structure of Israel.

sens: Man of the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy
H3275.detail: Jaecan is a chief of the tribe of Gad mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:13. He is part of a list of seven important chiefs of this tribe, all brothers, sons of Abihail. His name means "troublesome" (one who causes trouble or affliction), which may reflect the challenges that the Gadites faced during the period of the divided monarchy in Israel.
H3275.origine: The name Jaecan means "troublesome" or "one who brings trouble." It is a typical Hebrew name from the time of the divided monarchy. The genealogical context shows that he is part of an important family of the tribe of Gad, which had received its inheritance east of the Jordan.
H3275.emploi: Jaecan appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:13. He is listed among the seven sons of Abihail and the principal chiefs of the tribe of Gad. This genealogical enumeration is part of the records of the tribes of Israel, which document the lineages and administrative organization of the Hebrew people during the time of the divided monarchy. His mention, though brief, attests to the importance of his family in the political and religious life of Gad.

sens: To be useful, to have a beneficial effect, to provide an advantage
To produce a profit, a material or moral gain
To be of no help, to provide nothing (used negatively)
H3276.detail:
1. The word expresses the idea that something is useful or effective for accomplishing something. It refers to the concrete utility of an object or an action. In Isaiah 44:9, the manufactured idols "are of no use": they cannot help those who worship them.

2. The word also denotes the profit or advantage one derives from something — not only material but also spiritual or moral. In Proverbs 11:4, wealth "is of no use" on the day of judgment; only righteousness delivers.

3. Very often, the verb is used in the negative form to indicate that something is completely useless, vain, or ineffective. In 1 Samuel 12:21, false deities "bring neither profit nor deliverance," emphasizing the urgency of not following them. Jeremiah 7:8 reiterates this idea: deceptive hopes "are of no use."
H3276.origine: The Hebrew verb יָעַל comes from a root that fundamentally means "to be strong, to have strength." That is why it comes to mean "to have power over something," "to be effective." The form used here (Hiphil) adds the idea of "to make serve," "to make profit." This verb belongs to the family of words expressing utility and effectiveness in the Hebrew language.
H3276.emploi: The verb appears 21 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs) and among the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah). It is almost always used negatively or interrogatively: "What is the use of this?" or "It is of no use." Biblical authors use it to show the futility of idols (Isaiah 44:9), the ineffectiveness of bad alliances (Isaiah 30:5-6), or the vanity of seeking wealth or security outside of God. In Job 15:3 and 21:15, Job and his friends debate what it means to "serve God": does having a relationship with God bring profit? This is an existential question for suffering men.
H3276.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on what truly matters in their life. The Bible uses it to show that wealth, idols, and false gods are ultimately vain and unhelpful. It calls to seek what truly "serves" — that is, justice, faithfulness to God, and His word. For the Christian, it is an invitation to evaluate their priorities: what truly has weight and effectiveness in eternity?

sens: Wild ruminant mammal of the mountains, with a stocky body and curved horns
Biblical symbol of agility and skill in moving in high places
H3277G.detail:
1. The wild goat is an animal of mountainous regions, capable of climbing with agility on steep rocks. In 1 Samuel 24:3, it refers to the rocky heights where David hides from Saul's pursuit: "on the rocks of the wild goats" evokes inaccessible places where only an agile animal that can climb well could survive.
2. The wild goat becomes the image of liveliness, the ability to move where others cannot go. That is why the psalmists and prophets will use this creature to evoke divine swiftness or the lightness of one who escapes danger.
H3277G.origine: The Hebrew word ya.el literally describes this mountain animal. It belongs to the family of caprids, these wild goats and ibexes that populated the high plateaus. The root expresses agility and elevation: a being that ascends, climbs, rises on peaks. Other Semitic languages have similar words to designate these creatures of the heights.
H3277G.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond, in 1 Samuel 24:3. Saul pursues David in the wilderness of Judah. The text situates the scene on the "rocks of the wild goats" — not to enumerate the local fauna, but to emphasize the inaccessibility of the place: it is terrain where the most agile animals can barely live. David finds refuge there, illustrating both his ingenuity and the impossible situation Saul has pushed him into. The use of the wild goat thus serves to enhance the atmosphere of the narrative: the untamed and dangerous heights.
H3277G.portee: The wild goat reminds the reader of God's protective power in the face of persecution. Just as this animal finds refuge on rocky heights where no one can reach it, David discovers that there are places where human malice cannot follow him. It is an invitation to recognize that God reserves unexpected refuges for us when threats draw near.

sens: Mountain animal, a species of wild goat or ibex found in rocky regions
Free and agile creature, symbol of untamed nature
H3277H.detail:
1. The word designates an animal of the highlands, related to the domestic goat but living wild in the rocky mountains of the ancient Near East. It is a robust animal, adapted to steep terrains: in Job 39:4, God asks Job if he knows when these wild goats give birth to their young, highlighting their hidden and free life, far from human control.
2. By extension, the animal embodies freedom and untamed nature, independence from man. In Psalms 104:18, the high rocks are described as the refuge of wild goats, an image of creatures that find their security away from civilization, in the domain that God has established for them.
H3277H.origine: The Hebrew word יָעֵל (ya'el) comes from a root related to agility and lightness of movement in difficult terrains. It specifically designates the wild animal, distinct from the domestic goat (עֵז, ëz). It is a well-known animal in ancient Syria-Palestine, admired for its ability to climb and live in spaces where man cannot survive.
H3277H.emploi: The word appears twice in the Old Testament, both in poetic and contemplative contexts: in Job 39:4, during God's discourse to Job, and in Psalms 104:18, in a hymn of praise to creation. In both cases, the wild goat illustrates the marvelous order that God has created, where each creature has its place and means of living, independently of man. The word is never used to evoke a domestic goat or a service rendered to man: it always evokes wild and free nature.
H3277H.portee: The wild goat invites us to recognize that God cares for all His creatures, even those we do not see and cannot control. These two texts reveal divine wisdom in creation: each animal has its place, its food, its refuge, without depending on our help. Meditating on this strengthens our trust: the God who feeds the wild goats of the mountains also cares for us.

sens: Wife of the Kenite Heber, who killed the Canaanite general Sisera
H3278.detail: Jael is a woman living during the time of the Judges, before the Israelite monarchy. She is the wife of Heber the Kenite. During the battle between Israel and the Canaanites, the enemy general Sisera flees and seeks refuge in her tent. Jael receives him with hospitality (Judges 4:18), hides him under a blanket, and while he falls asleep from exhaustion, she drives a tent peg into his temple, killing him (Judges 4:21). This unexpected act by a woman becomes decisive for Israel's victory. The song of Deborah celebrates Jael as "blessed among women" (Judges 5:24), acknowledging her role in Israel's deliverance.
H3278.origine: The name means "mountain goat" or "gazelle," evoking the agility and lightness of this mountain creature. It is a Hebrew name that perhaps emphasizes the liveliness and boldness of this remarkable woman.
H3278.emploi: Jael appears six times in the book of Judges, entirely in chapters 4 and 5: four times in chapter 4 (verses 17, 18, 21, 22) which recount the events in detail, and then twice in chapter 5 (verses 6 and 24) in the victory song sung by Deborah after the battle. The account in chapter 4 emphasizes her courageous action and paradoxical hospitality — welcoming the enemy to better eliminate him. The song in chapter 5 makes her a heroine, calling her "the woman who lived in tents" and blessing her among all women.
H3278.portee: Jael illustrates a profound truth: God can use unexpected people, including a woman foreign to the people of Israel, to accomplish His deliverance. Her story teaches that courage and faith are not measured by physical strength, but by trust in God and determination. It also shows how God honors those who serve His purposes, even in surprising ways.

sens: Man from the time of exile and return
Head of a family among the descendants of Solomon's servants
Ancestor of a family that returned from captivity with Zerubbabel
H3279.detail: Jaala is a man mentioned in the lists of families that returned from exile in Babylon during the return to Judah under the leadership of Zerubbabel. He was the head of a family whose members descended from the servants who had served in the court of King Solomon. His name appears twice in the biblical records: once in Ezra 2:56 and again in Nehemiah 7:58, in parallel lists enumerating the families of "servants" or descendants of Solomon's servants who participated in the return. These lists served to establish the genealogy and identity of the families authorized to resettle in Judea.
H3279.origine: The name Jaala means "who ascends" or "ascent" in Hebrew, evoking the image of a climb. It is a meaningful name that reflects the hope of return: these families ascending from Babylon to Judea were literally making a spiritual and geographical "ascent" to the promised land. The name was borne by a man living during one of the most significant periods in Israel's history, that of restoration after exile.
H3279.emploi: Jaala is mentioned only once by this name in the lists of the return from exile: in Ezra 2:56 and its parallel in Nehemiah 7:58. These two passages are part of detailed genealogical records enumerating the families that returned from Babylonian captivity around 538 BC. Jaala's family was significant enough to merit a nominal mention in these official records, alongside other families of temple servants and royal court members. The fact that his name appears in two parallel sources confirms the authenticity of his existence and the importance of his lineage.

sens: Small, slender, agile, and graceful antelope with sweet and expressive eyes
Poetic figure of feminine beauty and delicate elegance
H3280.detail:
1. The gazelle is a small wild antelope, light and fast, known for its graceful silhouette and large, sweet eyes. In Proverbs 5:19, it symbolizes a beautiful and alluring woman: "Be intoxicated always in her love, be exhilarated always with her love" — the image suggests both the sweetness of the gaze and irresistible attraction.
2. Figuratively, the gazelle becomes a poetic metaphor to express feminine beauty and tender love. Its agility, lightness, and natural grace make it the ideal symbol of what is beautiful, light, and captivating.
H3280.origine: The Hebrew word יַעֲלָה (yaala) literally refers to a female ibex or gazelle. It is related to the verb עלה (ala), which means "to ascend" or "to go up" — a likely reference to the agility of the animal that climbs effortlessly on rocky slopes. This term thus evokes both the real animal and its characteristic qualities: elegance, lightness, and the ability to move gracefully.
H3280.emploi: The word appears only once in the text of the Segond (in Proverbs 5:19), where it is used poetically to refer to a beloved wife. In this sapiential and poetic context, the gazelle symbolizes not the animal itself, but feminine beauty and seduction. The image is particularly clear: the wise man exhorts the man to find pleasure in marital love, comparing his wife to a gazelle full of charms — graceful, delicate, and captivating.
H3280.portee: This verse helps the Christian understand that marital love and physical attraction between spouses are intended by God and dignified. The gazelle is not a banal image: it expresses beauty and admiration in their noblest and most joyful form, inviting the husband to appreciate his wife with wonder and fidelity.

sens: Son of Esau and Oholibamah, one of the Edomite chiefs of old
H3281.detail: Jaelam is an Edomite man, son of Esau (the ancestor of the Edomites) and Oholibamah. He appears in the genealogical lists of the sons of Esau, notably in Genesis 36:5 where he is named among the children born to Esau in the land of Canaan. In Genesis 36:18, he is presented as an Edomite chief, confirming his importance in Esau's lineage. His brothers are Jeush and Korah (children of his mother Oholibamah), while his half-brothers are Eliphaz and Reuel.
H3281.origine: The name Jaelam means "hidden" or "concealed" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking an idea of protection or reserve. It is a characteristic name of the Edomite line, linked to the lineage of Esau, whose generations are traced in the genealogical lists of Genesis. The name appears in the same genealogical contexts as his Edomite brothers and half-brothers.
H3281.emploi: Jaelam is mentioned four times in Scripture, always in genealogical lists: twice in Genesis 36 (verses 5 and 14) among the sons of Esau born in Canaan, once in Genesis 36:18 where he is designated as a chief, and once in 1 Chronicles 1:35 in a parallel enumeration of Esau's descendants. These mentions serve to clearly identify him as one of Esau's important sons and confirm his status as a chief among the Edomites in ancient times.

sens: introduces the reason or motive for an action, a judgment, a consequence
expresses the cause of a situation or a state of affairs
marks the intention or basis of a divine decision
H3282.detail:
1. This word introduces the reason why something happens or is done: the cause or motive that explains an action. Thus in Genesis 22:16, God blesses Abraham "because" he was obedient and did not withhold his son. This is the explanation of the why.
2. It also expresses the cause of a concrete situation or state: what has provoked a change. Ezekiel 28:2 states that the prince of Tyre sinned "because" his heart was lifted up, meaning that this feeling of pride is the reason for his fall.
3. Sometimes it marks the basis of a decision or a divine word: God acts or speaks "because" such a thing has happened or such an intention exists. In 2 Chronicles 6:8, God approves David "since" he intended to build a house for His name.
H3282.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of "responding" or "saying in return": it thus introduces the answer to the implicit question "why?". In the Old Testament, it is the most common conjunction to express causality. It appears 94 times and structures the logic of prophetic and legislative texts.
H3282.emploi: יַעַן appears 94 times in the Old Testament, especially in the historical and prophetic books (particularly Ezekiel and Jeremiah). It almost always introduces an explanation: the reason for a blessing or a curse, a divine judgment, a promise, or a condemnation. Very frequent in divine discourse ("Thus says the Lord: Because...") this word shapes the biblical theology of judgment according to works. The Segond translates it mainly as "because" or "since", depending on whether the cause is prior or simultaneous.
H3282.portee: This word reminds the reader that nothing happens by chance in God's design: every action has a reason, every judgment is just and explained. Understanding the biblical "because" helps the Christian see the coherence of the divine plan and recognize that God never acts without motive. It is an invitation to examine our own actions in light of divine justice and mercy.

sens: Large desert bird, fast runner, unable to fly
Animal declared unclean according to Mosaic law
H3283.detail:
1. The ostrich is a large bird that lives in desert regions. Unlike most birds, it cannot fly, but it runs at high speed on the sand. It is an animal that the Israelites were well acquainted with, as it inhabited the deserts near their land. In Lamentations 4:3, it is mentioned as a creature of the desert.
2. According to the law of Moses, the ostrich was classified among ritually unclean animals, meaning it was not to be eaten or touched for religious reasons. This status was part of the rules that distinguished God's people from other nations.
H3283.origine: The Hebrew word יָעֵן (yaen) specifically designates the ostrich. Its exact etymology is uncertain, but it may be related to a word that imitates the harsh cry of the animal. This word appears in several biblical texts and in Akkadian with a similar meaning. The ostrich was well known in the ancient Near East.
H3283.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Lamentations 4:3, where the prophet Jeremiah cruelly compares the daughter of Judah to the ostriches of the desert. This comparison illustrates the lack of maternal compassion of the nation towards its children, the poet using the image of this desert bird, known for its natural indifference, to reinforce his accusation of hardness of heart.
H3283.portee: This image of the ostrich reminds us that biblical laments do not hesitate to compare God's people to unclean or repulsive animals to express the weight of divine judgment. It is a call to take seriously the consequences of sin and to return to the tenderness of the Lord.

sens: Large desert running bird, with gray or black plumage
Unclean animal according to Mosaic law
Creature inhabiting desolate and abandoned places
Symbol of desolation and ruin
H3284.detail:
1. The ostrich is a large desert bird, unable to fly despite its wings. It appears in the lists of unclean animals in the Mosaic law (Leviticus 11:16; Deuteronomy 14:15), alongside other birds like the owl and the seagull.
2. As an unclean animal, the ostrich cannot be consumed by the people of Israel: it is listed among the creatures whose flesh defiles those who eat it.
3. In prophetic passages, the ostrich becomes the typical inhabitant of ruins and destroyed cities. Isaiah 13:21 and 34:13 show it taking possession of ruined palaces and devastated strongholds, alongside jackals and owls — an image of a civilization reduced to nothing.
4. The ostrich symbolizes extreme desolation: when Job laments (30:29), he compares himself to the brother of jackals and the companion of ostriches, expressing total degradation. However, the prophecy in Isaiah 43:20 associates it with the glorification of God in the desert restored by His grace, showing that even wild creatures celebrate His salvation.
H3284.origine: The Hebrew word יַעֲנָה likely comes from a root evoking the cry or lamentation. The term also appears in the form of "daughter of the voice" or "mourner" in some ancient traditions. The ostrich was well known to the ancient Hebrews as a creature of the Arabian desert and was associated with abandoned places and ruins. The Hebrew root reveals the image of a vocal creature — the ostrich indeed makes deep and prolonged cries that fill the desert.
H3284.emploi: The word appears 8 times, almost exclusively in the context of purity laws or prophecies of ruin. Leviticus 11:16 and Deuteronomy 14:15 classify it among the unclean birds that Israel cannot eat. The prophecies of Isaiah (13:21; 34:13; 43:20) and the laments of Job (30:29) place it in devastated or abandoned places: it embodies the desolation of a judged land. Jeremiah 50:39 and Micah 1:8 reinforce this image of prophetic desolation. Depending on the contexts, the ostrich is either the legally unclean animal or the living symbol of lands ruined by God's judgment.
H3284.portee: The ostrich reminds biblical readers that God classifies creatures and establishes laws of separation between clean and unclean, just as He separates His people from the nations. In prophecies of judgment, it becomes a visible sign of the overturning of human civilizations — only wild creatures survive there, which shows the total neglect reserved for the rebels. Conversely, in Isaiah 43:20, it glorifies God in the restored places, reminding that messianic salvation will restore all that has been ravaged.

sens: Chief of the tribe of Gad during the time of the divided monarchy
H3285.detail: Jaenaï is a character from the Old Testament belonging to the tribe of Gad. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogical account of the book of Chronicles, where he appears among the important leaders of his tribe at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two.
H3285.origine: The name Jaenaï means "the one whom Jehovah answers" or "God answers". It is composed of the Hebrew verb עָנָה (to answer, to hear) and the divine name יָהּ (Yah, a short form of Jehovah). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God within it, which was common among the Israelites.
H3285.emploi: Jaenaï is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:12, where he is listed among the chief leaders of the tribe of Gad in Bashan. The text places him after Joel and Shapham in a list of notables from his tribe. This unique mention in a genealogical record reveals his local importance as a recognized chief or officer among the Gadites, although the details of his life are not reported to us.

sens: To experience physical fatigue, to lose strength
To be exhausted, at the end of one's strength
To be weary, weakened in effort
Figuratively: to accomplish something in vain, without result
H3286.detail:
1. To tire oneself out means to experience physical fatigue, to feel one's strength decline during prolonged effort. This is what the young man who works hard experiences: "Even youths grow tired and weary" (Isaiah 40:30). The blacksmith who forges an axe becomes so exhausted that he loses his energy (Isaiah 44:12).
2. To be exhausted means to reach the point where one has no more strength, where the body can no longer continue. One who works without drinking or eating finds themselves "exhausted" (Isaiah 44:12), drained of all vigor.
3. This word also denotes a state of moral fatigue, discouragement: to feel weary from effort. But it is distinguished from simple weariness by its intensity — it is a fatigue that truly weakens.
4. Figuratively, it also means to work in vain, without achieving anything: "The peoples have labored in vain, the nations have grown weary for nothing" (Jeremiah 51:58) — the effort expended to build Babylon was useless since everything burned down.
H3286.origine: The Hebrew verb יָעֵף (ya'aph) refers to the idea of seeing one's strength diminish, to weaken under weight. It belongs to a family of words evoking physical and moral weariness. The root suggests the image of a body that can no longer keep up, that "sags" under fatigue. The word is common in wisdom texts and prophecies, notably in Isaiah where it contrasts with God's inexhaustible strength.
H3286.emploi: This verb appears 9 times in the Bible, primarily in the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Habakkuk, Daniel). It first describes the common human experience: the fatigue of young people, of the blacksmith who works hard. Isaiah also uses it to affirm that God never tires (40:28) — He does not "tire" or grow weary. The prophet uses it in contrast: men tire, but those who trust in the Lord renew their strength (40:31). Jeremiah uses the word ironically: the peoples have tired themselves building Babylon in vain, since everything will perish by fire.
H3286.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to meditate on two realities: on one hand, fatigue is an authentic experience, inherent to fragile human nature; on the other hand, it is not our final word. Those who put their trust in God "renew their strength" and "do not tire." It is a word of hope for all who are weary and seem not to progress: the Lord is never exhausted and can revitalize those who turn to Him.

sens: Physically exhausted from effort or travel
Weakened, without strength
Morally discouraged, downcast
H3287.detail:
1. The word describes physical exhaustion after prolonged effort or a long journey. In Judges 8:15, Gideon speaks of his men who are tired after the battle, and in 2 Samuel 16:2, wine is prepared to refresh those who will be tired in the wilderness — it is the fatigue of the body that needs rest and nourishment.
2. Beyond simple fatigue, the word can denote a deeper weakening, a failure of strength. Isaiah 40:29 expresses this well: "He gives strength to the weary" — it is a weakness that requires help, an external intervention to be restored.
3. The word can also evoke moral or spiritual exhaustion, a discouragement that weighs on the person, not only the body but the soul in decline.
H3287.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of wearing out, losing strength. It is found in several contexts in the Old Testament to describe exhaustion after effort or trial. It is a concrete word that speaks of the vulnerability of the human body and soul in the face of life's demands.
H3287.emploi: This word appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first used in historical accounts to describe the physical state of warriors or travelers after effort (Judges 8:15, 2 Samuel 16:2). Isaiah uses it twice, notably in 40:29 where he contrasts it with the strength that God provides — it is a contrast between human weakness and divine power. The context is always that of people in difficulty who need help, food, water, or renewed strength.
H3287.portee: This word reminds us that physical fatigue and exhaustion are not flaws, but a human reality. But Isaiah 40:29 tells us that God does not leave the weary without help: He gives strength to the one who collapses. It is a word of comfort for the tested believer: our exhaustion does not escape God, who can restore and strengthen us.

sens: Great speed, swiftness of movement
Promptness to act
Ease, lightness in the accomplishment of an action
H3288.detail:
1. The word primarily describes great speed or swiftness of movement: it is the absence of slowness, the ability to cover distance quickly. The image is that of Gabriel's swift flight approaching the prophet Daniel "in swift flight" at dusk (Daniel 9:21), like a bird cutting through the air effortlessly.
2. It also evokes promptness, diligence: doing something without dragging or hesitating, with a sort of natural eagerness. It is the efficiency of one who acts without wasting time.
3. By extension, it can express ease and lightness: one who moves with speed does so effortlessly, almost without fatigue — hence the Hebrew word also expresses a kind of freshness, the absence of breathlessness.
H3288.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means properly "to fly" or "to rush." Its basic image is that of airy, light, and rapid movement: the bird that flies effortlessly represents what is done without heaviness or delay. The source definition speaks of "weariness," which may seem contrary, but it reflects the opposite idea: an action performed with such lightness and speed that it does not tire the one who accomplishes it.
H3288.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 9:21, where the angel Gabriel approaches the prophet Daniel "in swift flight" while he is praying. It is a moment of solemn revelation: Gabriel does not appear slowly or heavily, but with supernatural speed, emphasizing the urgency and gravity of the divine message he brings. The Segond translates here as "swift" to convey this notion of miraculous speed and promptness.
H3288.portee: This word speaks to the speed with which God intervenes in history and in the lives of believers. Gabriel coming "in swift flight" teaches that God does not delay in responding to sincere prayer: His answer comes promptly, at the precise moment it is awaited. For the reader, it is an invitation to trust: the Lord does not move with slowness or indifference.

sens: To give advice, a recommendation to someone to help them act
To deliberate together, exchange opinions to make a decision collectively
To form a plan, a design in the mind before acting
To conspire together against someone
H3289.detail:
1. To give counsel is to offer someone a wise word to guide them. This is what Moses does: he gives Joshua advice on how to govern the people (Exodus 18:19). A counselor is one who possesses this wisdom and whom one consults: King Rehoboam hesitates between the counsel of the elders and that of the young men (1 Kings 12:6-13), and this is a turning point for his reign.
2. Sometimes, several people deliberate together to find the best decision. Job ironically says that one who understands nothing also gives their "counsel," as if they were participating in a common reflection (Job 26:3). The Lord also affirms that He sits with His counselors in His wisdom: "Only He has formed the counsel, and His thought has been executed" (Isaiah 14:24, 14:26).
3. The word also means design or plan: a noble design endures (Isaiah 32:8), while a wicked plan is a secret scheme. It is the plan that one matures in their heart before executing it.
4. Finally, the word also expresses conspiracy, a secret alliance against an enemy: the enemies of Jerusalem consult together to destroy it (Psalms 83:4-6), or Absalom "consults" Ahithophel to overthrow David (2 Samuel 15:12).
H3289.origine: The Hebrew root יעץ (ya'ats) comes from a very ancient image: that of the bond that unites those who speak to each other, who embrace. Counsel is primarily an act of closeness and mutual listening. The same root has produced the word עצה (etsah), the counsel itself — what is advised. It also appears in the names of ancient tribes and advisory associations. This root emphasizes that wisdom comes through dialogue: one can only counsel well face to face, weighing words together.
H3289.emploi: This verb appears 73 times in the Old Testament, especially in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs, Psalms). It is also concentrated among the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel). Moses, David, the kings, and the prophets regularly employ counselors. The meaning of the word changes according to the context: a just counsel brings together and saves (1 Kings 12:6, where the elders give good counsel), while a bad counsel or conspiracy divides and destroys (2 Samuel 15:12, Psalms 83:4). The Lord Himself is presented as the only true unshakeable counselor (Isaiah 40:14, Isaiah 45:21), whose counsel cannot be overturned.
H3289.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that wise decisions do not come from a single isolated person. God invites us to seek the counsel of wise individuals who fear the Lord, and to humbly receive correction. Proverbs repeats that "without counsel, one fails, but with a multitude of counselors, one succeeds" (Proverbs 15:22). This also invites us to recognize that God alone possesses perfect and eternal counsel, and that straying from His word leads to losing oneself in vain conspiracies.

sens: Son of Isaac and Rebekah, grandson of Abraham
He who obtained the birthright and his father's blessing through deceit
He whose name was changed to Israel after wrestling with God at Peniel
Ancestor of the twelve tribes of Israel and father of the founding patriarchs
H3290.detail:
1. Jacob is the younger son of Isaac and Rebekah, twin brother of Esau. His name literally means "he who holds the heel" or "supplanter," because he was born holding onto his brother's heel (Genesis 25:26). He is the grandson of Abraham, heir to the divine promise made to his descendants.

2. Jacob deceitfully obtains the birthright from his brother Esau by offering him a meal in exchange for it (Genesis 25:34), and then he usurps the paternal blessing reserved for the firstborn by disguising himself before his blind father Isaac (Genesis 27). This deceit forces him to flee from Esau's anger to Haran.

3. Throughout his tumultuous life, Jacob has a decisive encounter with God at Peniel, where he wrestles all night with a divine angel and receives the new name Israel, "he who has wrestled with God" (Genesis 32). This moment marks his spiritual transformation and his subsequent reconciliation with his brother.

4. Jacob has twelve sons and one daughter who become the ancestors of the twelve tribes of Israel: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Dinah, and Benjamin with Rachel, and Joseph with Rachel as well (Genesis 29-30).
H3290.origine: The name Jacob (יַעֲקֹב) comes from a Hebrew root meaning "heel" (עָקֵב). The popular etymology in the account of Genesis 25:26 plays on this double meaning: Jacob is born grasping Esau's heel, and his name evokes both the physical gesture and the idea of "supplanting" or taking someone else's place. This name reflects the character of the individual: cunning, ambitious, but also transformed by divine grace that elevates him despite his flaws.
H3290.emploi: Jacob appears more than 320 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in Genesis where his entire story unfolds. The text first shows him as an obedient son sent to find a wife in Mesopotamia (Genesis 28), then working fourteen years for Laban and gradually acquiring wealth and family through his industriousness (Genesis 29-30). The Psalms and the prophets (Isaiah 49:6, Psalms 78:21) invoke the name of Jacob to refer to the entire people of Israel, sometimes in parallel with the name "Israel" itself. Thus, Jacob represents both an individual man and the collective identity of God's chosen people.
H3290.portee: Jacob embodies for the believer the possibility of spiritual transformation despite flaws and missteps. Although born cunning and deceitful, he becomes the father of God's people and receives the renewed divine promise. His story teaches that God does not withdraw from those who seek Him, even imperfectly, and that He can redirect an entire life toward His purpose. The name "Jacob" reminds the biblical reader that God works not through human perfection, but through His grace.

sens: A man of the tribe of Simeon
H3291.detail: 1. Jaakob is a man belonging to the tribe of Simeon, a descendant of Jacob. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of family leaders of Simeon during the time of the divided monarchy (1 Chronicles 4:36).
H3291.origine: The name Jaakob literally means "toward Jacob" or "in the direction of Jacob." It reflects the importance of Jacob, the founding ancestor of all Israel, in the genealogy and identity of the Simeonite people. The name emphasizes the genealogical link with Jacob, ancestor of all Israelites.
H3291.emploi: Jaakob appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 4:36, where he is listed among the family leaders recorded during a census of the tribe of Simeon at the time of the divided monarchy of Israel. His inclusion in this genealogical list suggests that he was a person of some importance in his tribe, worthy of being recorded in the history of Israel.

sens: A man from the time of the patriarchs
Son of Etser and brother of Bilhan and Zaavan
Edomite
H3292.detail: 1. Jaakan is a man who lived during the time of the patriarchs, mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Edom. 2. He is the son of Etser and the brother of Bilhan and Zaavan, all three appearing in the list of Edomite family leaders (1 Chronicles 1:42). 3. Jaakan belongs to the Edomite people, that is, the descendants of Esau, the twin brother of Jacob. His name and that of his family appear in the ancient genealogies that trace the lineages of the pre-flood and patriarchal peoples.
H3292.origine: The name Jaakan comes from Hebrew and means "may he oppress them" or "one who oppresses." It is an Edomite name borne by a member of the family of Etser, included in the genealogical lists of Edom that date back to the ancient times of the patriarchs.
H3292.emploi: Jaakan is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 1:42, where he appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Edom. He is presented as the son of Etser alongside his brothers Bilhan and Zaavan. This mention is part of a genealogical account that lists the leaders and families of Edom in ancient days, without further detail about his life or actions.

sens: Dense wooded area covered with trees
Set of wood or forest material
Deserted and wild place, refuge or hiding place
Difficult-to-access territory, uncivilized domain
H3293A.detail: 1. A forest is primarily a large expanse of land covered with tightly packed trees. It is a natural space where vegetation dominates: Deuteronomy 19:5 speaks of a man cutting wood in the forest, meaning he is felling a tree among many others. 2. The word also refers to wood as a material and resource: one goes there to obtain wood (Joshua 17:15 invites to clear the forest). 3. The forest is a wild, sparsely inhabited place where fierce beasts reign: Jeremiah 12:8 compares God's inheritance to a lion in the forest that roars. It is a place of danger and refuge at the same time, as when David hides in the forest (1 Samuel 22:5). 4. The forest also symbolizes an untamed territory that man must conquer or transform: Isaiah 32:15 announces that the desert will become fertile when the Spirit of God is poured out, and the orchard will be considered a forest, meaning a space of wealth and abundant life.
H3293A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root related to the image of a dense, thick, bristly place. It belongs to the same family as wood or brush. The forest evokes in the Old Testament both a resource (timber, shelter) and a danger (wild beasts, uncontrolled space). It is an element of the Palestinian landscape that well reflects the raw nature, before human civilization.
H3293A.emploi: The word forest appears about 48 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical, poetic, and prophetic books. It primarily designates a real geographical place: the forest where wood is chopped (Deuteronomy 19:5), that of Lebanon known for its magnificent cedars (Isaiah 37:24), or the forests of the territory of Israel that the conquering tribes must clear (Joshua 17:15, 17:18). The forest is also the domain of wild beasts (Jeremiah 5:6, Amos 3:4): it breathes, cries out with joy before the Lord (1 Chronicles 16:33, Psalms 96:12). It becomes a poetic image of abandonment or devastation: Isaiah 10:18-19 speaks of the Lord consuming the forests in a short time. Finally, it symbolizes a space that must be conquered or transformed: Isaiah 29:17 and 32:15 announce that one day the barren desert will be transformed into a fertile forest by divine intervention.
H3293A.portee: For the biblical reader, the forest represents both God's raw creation, rich in resources and beauty (it praises the Lord), and the world waiting to be ordered, inhabited, and dominated by man as God's steward. It reminds us that God masters the wild nature and can transform it according to His will: moving from desert to forest is moving from death to life. The forest also invites us to recognize that every space in the world belongs to God and that man must be its faithful steward.

sens: Wooded area covered with trees
Wild place where natural honey abounds
Remote and difficult-to-access location
Image of refuge or hidden wealth
H3293B.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a forest in the literal sense: a large expanse covered with thick trees. In 1 Samuel 14:25-26, during the battle against the Philistines, Saul forbids his people from eating during the fight; but the forest they advance into is so rich in wild honey that it flows on the ground — an image of the natural abundance that a forest contains.
2. By extension, the word can specifically refer to a honeycomb found in the forest, as in Song of Solomon 5:1 where the lover says, "I eat my honeycomb"; here the forest is not described, but the honey found there symbolizes the sweetness and richness that one gathers.
H3293B.origine: The Hebrew word ya'ar comes from a root that evokes the idea of something dense, tight, intertwined — the branches and trunks of a forest. It belongs to the concrete vocabulary of rural and agrarian life in Israel. The word is used both for a real forest and for the places where it provides its natural products (honey, wood).
H3293B.emploi: The word appears 3 times in the provided passages: 2 times in 1 Samuel 14 where it literally designates the forest where Saul pursues the Philistines, a natural place from which honey springs; 1 time in Song of Solomon where it evokes rather the poetic image of precious honey. In Samuel, it is a real, inhabited, dangerous, and rich forest; in Song of Solomon, the word melts into an image of love where honey — a product of the forest — becomes a metaphor for marital sweetness.
H3293B.portee: The forest reminds us that creation is full of riches that God has hidden for His people. In 1 Samuel, it shows that even in the midst of battle and danger, the Lord provides — honey springs from the ground without being cultivated. In Song of Solomon, the forest becomes the symbol of an inexhaustible wealth of love to taste and share.

sens: Honey-filled wax structure produced by bees
Honey itself or sweet food
Sweetness, pleasantness of speech or words
H3293G.detail: 1. The honeycomb is the structure that bees build with wax to store honey and raise their larvae. It is the concrete image of the word: the cells aligned regularly, filled with golden honey. 2. By extension, the word designates honey itself or the sweet food it produces, which is good to eat. 3. Figuratively, honey becomes a symbol of what is sweet, pleasant, and tasty: sweet words, sugary language that pleases the ear. This is why, in the Bible, wise or kind words are often compared to honey to show their sweetness (as in Proverbs 24:13 where honey symbolizes wisdom that is sweet to the soul's palate).
H3293G.origine: The Hebrew word יַעַר comes from a root that evokes the production and accumulation of honey. In biblical Hebrew, this word specifically designates the honeycomb with its wax structure. It is also found in the context of the regularly organized cells that bees build. The word is rare in the Bible and mainly appears in poetic texts where it serves as an image of sweetness.
H3293G.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 132:6, where it speaks of finding the Ark of the Covenant "in the fields of Jaar." There, יַעַר seems to be an ancient place name (a variant of Kiriath-jearim), rather than the word for honeycomb. Although the Masoretic text presents here a proper name, the root of the word retains its etymological link with the image of the honeycomb and what is sweet, accumulated, and ordered. The context is that of the quest for the Ark, a symbol of divine presence.
H3293G.portee: Honey reminds us that the Word of God is sweet: its promises comfort, its commandments soothe the heart that receives them with trust. Just as the honeycomb is the fruit of the patient work of bees, divine wisdom is a treasure to be sought with perseverance.

sens: Region covered with dense trees and underbrush
Figuratively, a confusing and tangled place, difficult to traverse
H3293H.detail:
1. The forest of Ephraim refers to a wooded area in the territory of Ephraim, in the West Bank. It is land covered with trees and dense vegetation, characteristic of the mountainous regions of Canaan. In 2 Samuel 18:6, it is on this rugged terrain that the battle takes place where Absalom, son of David, will be killed: the forest thus becomes the site of a military tragedy.
2. The image of the forest also evokes confusion and difficulty: it is a place where one can get lost, where visibility is limited, and where it is easy to fall into traps or ambushes. In the battle of Ephraim, it is precisely this difficult terrain that causes the debacle of Absalom's army.
H3293H.origine: The Hebrew word יַעַר (ya'ar) comes from a root that refers to the idea of density and entanglement. The forest is the space where trees are tightly packed together, where darkness and impenetrability reign. The word also appears in other biblical passages to designate wooded areas in the territory of Israel, always with this connotation of a wild and difficult-to-master place.
H3293H.emploi: The word יַעַר appears only once in the Hebrew Bible according to the provided usages, specifically in 2 Samuel 18:6, where it refers to the forest of Ephraim. It is the site of the battle between the armies of David and Absalom, a battle in which more than twenty thousand men fall. The forest is not merely a backdrop here: it is a crucial strategic element, where the difficult terrain plays a decisive role in the course of events.
H3293H.portee: This battle in the forest of Ephraim reminds the reader that even great military powers and earthly kingdoms remain subject to the sovereignty of God. The death of Absalom in this confusing place symbolizes the failure of the revolt against the order established by God. For the believer, it is a lesson in humility in the face of divine plans, which can overturn the most ambitious human plans.

sens: Wooded area, grove of trees
Building of Solomon called 'House of the Forest of Lebanon'
H3293I.detail:
1. A forest is a vast area covered with trees. The Hebrew word ya'ar simply designates this natural reality: thick woods, like those of Lebanon that provided cedar and cypress to the ancient kings of Israel.

2. In the time of Solomon, this term was used to name a monumental edifice built in Jerusalem. Called 'House of the Forest of Lebanon' (1 Kings 7:2), this structure was primarily a storage facility and a throne room: it contained the royal shields of gold (1 Kings 10:17), royal utensils (1 Kings 10:21), and served to store armors (Isaiah 22:8). It owed its name to its architectural decor: probably rows of cedar columns that evoked a forest of precious wood, reminiscent of the mountains of Lebanon from which the raw material came.
H3293I.origine: Ya'ar comes from a Hebrew root evoking the idea of covering, of becoming thick. The Hebrew word also appears in Aramaic and ancient Arabic with the same meaning: a covered land, densely wooded. In the Bible, it designates either the natural forest (Jeremiah 26:18) or, by extension, this unique building of Solomon that draws its prestige from the wood of Lebanon, the most renowned in the ancient Near East.
H3293I.emploi: The word forest (ya'ar) appears 6 times in the Segond, all related to Solomon's palace. In 1 Kings 7:2, it is the heart of the description: the king builds a 'house of the forest of Lebanon' equipped with four rows of cedar columns, set on this prestigious wood. In chapters 10 of 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles, it appears as the royal treasury where the gold shields and utensils are kept; in Isaiah 22:8, it is mentioned as a place of armament for the kingdom. The name 'forest' remains an architectural metaphor: Solomon transformed the cedar of Lebanon into a building, literally turning a forest into a royal dwelling.
H3293I.portee: This passage illustrates how the material wealth of Israel — including that of a prosperous and just king like Solomon — is ultimately fragile and fleeting. The mention of this sumptuous house alongside the warnings of the prophet Isaiah reminds the reader that gold, silver, and palaces do not guarantee security. This image invites us to reflect on what truly lasts in contrast to what fades: a constant biblical lesson on true priorities.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, descendant of Saul
H3294.detail: Jaera is a man who lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He belonged to the tribe of Benjamin and was a descendant of Saul. According to 1 Chronicles 9:42, he was the son of Ahaz and the father of Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri, thus continuing the genealogy of the Davidic royal dynasty.
H3294.origine: The name Jaera (יַעְרָה) means 'covered with forest' or 'wooded', probably referring to a physical or geographical trait. It is a variant or another name for Jehoaddah (יְהוֹעַדָּה), the same person appearing under this name in 1 Chronicles 8:36.
H3294.emploi: Jaera is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:42, in a genealogy of the descendants of Saul. He appears in the genealogical lists of the people returned from Babylonian exile. The same man is called Jehoaddah in 1 Chronicles 8:36, showing that biblical genealogies sometimes employed name variants for the same person.

sens: Honeycomb: the wax structure where bees store honey in the hive
H3295.detail: 1. The word refers to the honeycomb, that is, the hexagonal wax structure built by bees to store honey. In 1 Samuel 14:27, Jonathan dips the end of his staff into a honeycomb to taste it, which restores his strength and brightens his sight.
H3295.origine: The Hebrew word ya'arah comes from a root meaning 'forest' or 'wood'. The honeycomb is designated by this word probably because it evokes, through its branched and dense structure, a fabric of interwoven branches, like a miniature forest. It is a poetic image characteristic of biblical Hebrew.
H3295.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in 1 Samuel 14:27. It designates the honeycomb itself, not the honey that fills it. Jonathan, pursuing the Philistines, discovers a honeycomb in nature and tastes it despite the fast sworn by his father Saul. This passage illustrates the vitality that honey provides, a rich and energetic food highly valued in Israel.
H3295.portee: This passage reminds us that honey was in antiquity a precious food, synonymous with tasty and fortifying nourishment. The honeycomb also evokes the richness of the promised land, often described as 'a land flowing with milk and honey'. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to taste the goodness of God in the small delights of creation.

sens: Man of Bethlehem, father of Elhanan
Father of the warrior who killed Goliath
H3296.detail:
1. Jaaré-Oreguim is a man of Bethlehem mentioned only once in the Bible. His name literally means "forests of weaver" (or "forests of the one who weaves"), a Hebrew expression composed of two words. He is best known as the father of Elhanan, who is among the mighty warriors of David.
2. His son Elhanan performs a remarkable feat: he kills Goliath of Gath, the Philistine giant whose spear had a shaft like a weaver's beam (2 Samuel 21:19). This event places him at the heart of the accounts of the heroic battles fought under David's reign against the Philistines.
H3296.origine: The name Jaaré-Oreguim combines two Hebrew elements: "ya'ar" (forest) and "orguim" (weavers). This composite construction is characteristic of Hebrew nomenclature from the first millennium BCE. The character is also known by the name Jair (Yair in Hebrew). These name variants do not change the identity of the character but reflect the flexibility of the transmission of proper names in the oral and written traditions of ancient Israel.
H3296.emploi: Jaaré-Oreguim appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 21:19. He is presented there as the father of Elhanan, a warrior from Bethlehem in the service of David. The context is that of the wars fought between Israel and the Philistines during the period of the united monarchy. Although few details are given about Jaaré-Oreguim himself, his importance lies entirely in his connection with his son, whose warrior feat—the death of Goliath—immortalizes him alongside David's heroes.

sens: mountain on the northern border of Judah
H3297.detail: 1. Jearim is a mountain located on the northern boundary of the territory of Judah. It marks an important point in the description of the borders of the land assigned to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:10). It serves as a geographical landmark to precisely delineate which lands belong to Judah and which belong to neighboring tribes.
H3297.origine: The Hebrew name יְעָרִים (Jearim) comes from the root meaning "forests." This mountain was likely covered with woods, which gave it its name. The name Kesalon, which designates the same place, is another appellation for this same mountain on the borders of Judah.
H3297.emploi: This mountain appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:10, where it is included in the precise enumeration of the territorial limits granted to the tribe of Judah after the conquest. It is mentioned alongside other geographical landmarks such as Baala and Kesalon, in a description that follows the exact outline of the northern boundary of the territory of Judah.

sens: Benjamite mentioned only once in the genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin
H3298.detail: Jaaréschia is a man from the tribe of Benjamin, living during the time of the divided monarchy. He appears in the genealogical list of chapter 8 of 1 Chronicles, where he is named as one of the sons of Jerocham, alongside his brothers Elijah and Zicri (1 Chronicles 8:27). This character is known only from this single biblical mention, and we know nothing else about his life or deeds.
H3298.origine: The name Jaaréschia literally means "Jehovah nourishes" or "Jehovah supports." It is composed of two elements: "Jah" (Jehovah, the name of God) and "aresh," which evokes the idea of nourishing or supporting. It is a typical theophoric name of ancient Israel, expressing trust in divine providence.
H3298.emploi: Jaaréschia appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:27. He is listed in the detailed genealogy of the sons of Benjamin, recorded at a time when the tribes were reorganizing after the exile. His father is Jerocham, and his brothers include Elijah and Zicri. This genealogical mention attests to his existence and place in the Benjaminite lineage, although the Bible reports no events of his life.

sens: Man from the Exile and Return period
Descendant of Bani who married a foreign woman
H3299.detail: Jaasaï is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the Israelites returned from exile in Babylon. He appears in the list of descendants of Bani who, like many others at that time, had taken foreign wives (non-Israelite women). This practice was contrary to the Law, and the prophet Ezra urged them to send away these women to purify themselves and reconnect with God's covenant.
H3299.origine: The name Jaasaï literally means "they will do" in Hebrew, formed from the root of the verb "to do" (עשׂה). It is a theophoric or compound name that expresses an expected divine action. It reflects an ancient Hebrew practice of giving names that express a declaration or a prayer.
H3299.emploi: Jaasaï appears only once in the entire Bible, in Ezra 10:37. He is listed among the men whom the prophet Ezra gathered to lead them to repent of their marriages to foreign women. The context shows that after the return from the Babylonian exile, many Israelites had transgressed the Law by entering into these unions, and Ezra called upon all the men involved to acknowledge their wrongdoing and send away their foreign wives.

sens: To have the strength, abilities, or means to do something
To be able to overcome or defeat resistance
To be able to endure or withstand something
To succeed in accomplishing an action, achieving a goal
To have permission or legitimacy to do something
H3201.detail:
1. To have the strength, abilities, or means to do something: this is the physical, material, or moral capacity necessary to accomplish an action. When the possessions of Abraham and Lot become so significant that "they could not dwell together" (Genesis 13:6), it is because they lacked resources or space. Similarly, when Moses fears that he cannot bear the entire people alone (Numbers 11:14), he doubts he has the necessary strength.
2. To be able to overcome or defeat resistance: the word expresses victory, domination, the strength to prevail over an adversary. Deborah triumphs by saying, "Ask Barak if he can defeat us" (Judges 8:3). Balaam also refuses to curse Israel because he knows that God cannot be defeated (Numbers 22:6).
3. To be able to endure or withstand something: this is the strength of resistance in the face of a trial or limitation. The blind man Ahijah "could no longer see" (1 Kings 14:4): his body no longer had the capacity to see. The children of Israel "cannot withstand" their enemies (Joshua 7:12) because they have lost their spiritual strength.
4. To succeed in accomplishing an action, achieving a goal: this is the concrete ability to execute what one undertakes. Moses can "suffice" (Exodus 18:23) if he applies the advice of his father-in-law, meaning he has the strength to govern well.
5. To have permission or legitimacy to do something: the moral or legal context determines what is "permitted" or possible. Jeremiah says that the ears of the people "are unable to be attentive" (Jeremiah 6:10), not only physically but spiritually—they refuse to listen.
H3201.origine: The Hebrew verb יָכֹל (yakol) comes from an ancient root expressing strength, power, and capacity. The noun יָכִיל (yakil) is related, as is the Aramaic יְכִל (yekhel) which also means "to be able." The basic image is that of a force that bends or masters, capable of overcoming resistance or a limit. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this word is often translated by δύναμαι (dynamai), "to be able," which shares the same fundamental notion of power and capacity.
H3201.emploi: The verb yakol is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament (183 occurrences). It appears as early as Genesis and unfolds in all contexts of life: personal abilities, military strength, physical endurance, legal or moral power. In the narratives (Genesis, Exodus, Joshua, Judges, Samuel), it describes concrete situations: Abraham lacks space, Moses fears he cannot suffice, the Israelites lose their military strength. In the Psalms and the prophets, the word takes on a more theological tone: "power" becomes an expression of divine omnipotence in the face of human limits. Balaam cannot curse Israel because God prevents him (Numbers 22:6). The notion thus varies from simple "being able" to "having authority" or "being victorious."
H3201.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that true power comes from God and that our human strengths are limited. The texts where Israel "cannot" resist its enemies as long as it is under the weight of its sins (Joshua 7:12) teach that true victory depends on obedience and divine favor. Conversely, recognizing what one "cannot" do—overcome alone, understand spiritual matters, live righteously—invites one to turn to Him who can overcome all.

sens: to have the strength, ability, or skill to do something
to succeed in accomplishing, to achieve
to be able to (expresses a possibility or permission)
to have the authority or right to do something
H3202.detail: 1. This verb primarily expresses a concrete capacity: to have the strength or know-how necessary to accomplish an action. When the wise men of Babylon say to the king, "There is no one on earth who can tell what the king asks" (Daniel 2:10), they acknowledge that no mortal has the required skills. 2. The word also means "to succeed in" or "to achieve": Daniel was able (that is, succeeded in) to discover the secret of the king's dream (Daniel 2:47), which others could not do. 3. It can express a possibility or future capacity, often related to a promise or divine power. When the three young men assert, "Our God can deliver us from the fiery furnace" (Daniel 3:17), they declare that God has the power to intervene. 4. In a context of authority, the verb means "to have the right or permission to": only one who has this capacity can do it legally or legitimately.
H3202.origine: This Aramaic verb, found in the Aramaic portions of Daniel, expresses the fundamental idea of strength or power that allows one to accomplish something. The corresponding Hebrew root (יכל) has the same meaning: to be able, to have strength. The word belongs to the realm of the possible and impossible, the powerful and the weak, and it regularly appears in passages where divine power is contrasted with human helplessness.
H3202.emploi: This verb appears ten times in the book of Daniel, almost exclusively in Aramaic. It constantly recurs in scenes where Babylonian wise men or King Nebuchadnezzar acknowledge the limits of their wisdom and power in the face of divine mysteries. Daniel alone "can" interpret dreams (Daniel 2:27, 4:18), not because he is smarter, but because he possesses "the spirit of the holy gods." The verb also emphasizes God's own power: He can deliver (Daniel 3:17, 3:29), and no other god can do it like Him. It is a key word to show how true power resides in God alone.
H3202.portee: This verb teaches us that true ability comes from God, not from human wisdom or power. The Babylonian wise men, despite their reputation, recognize that they "cannot"—because the secret belongs to God alone. For the believer, this word reminds us that our limits are real, but our God has the power to accomplish what exceeds our strength. It is an invitation to trust in divine power rather than our own resources.

sens: to pour a liquid by letting it flow
to anoint by applying an oily substance
to desacralize by profane use
H3251.detail:
1. To pour out means to pour a liquid from a container by letting it flow: the holy anointing oil must remain reserved for its sacred use and must not be poured out on the bodies of ordinary men (Exodus 30:32).
2. The word evokes the action of anointing, that is, applying oil on someone or something to consecrate or bless it: to repaint this oil on any man would profane it.
3. To pour out can also mean to waste or desacralize: pouring the holy oil anywhere or on anyone would lose its sacred character and render it common.
H3251.origine: The verb יָסַךְ (yasakh) literally means to pour or to flow. It is related to the actions of pouring and anointing in the Old Testament. The word expresses the idea of letting a substance flow or spill, particularly oils or liquids reserved for religious or ritual uses.
H3251.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Exodus 30:32, regarding the holy anointing oil. The context is that of Mosaic legislation on sacred things: the oil must not be poured out (poured) on the body of an ordinary man, and one must not make a similar one. The usage is negative—a prohibition—and emphasizes the importance of respecting the separation between the sacred and the profane in Israelite worship.
H3251.portee: This word reminds the reader that the holiness of God requires a clear distinction between what is sacred and what is profane. The prohibition against pouring the holy oil elsewhere than where God ordains teaches respect for the limits that God establishes and the seriousness of profaning what is consecrated to Him. It is a lesson on obedience and reverence towards the things of God.
